title: Unit fractions: one equal part of a whole, or of a group

summary.text: Which is bigger, one third of a dosa or one eighth of the same dosa? Many people pick one eighth, because 8 is bigger than 3. In this lesson you cut paper strips and share out groundnuts to find the real answer. You learn to name and write fractions such as 1/3 and 1/8, and to find a fraction of a group, such as one quarter of 12. You also find out that a fraction has no size at all until someone says what the whole is.
summary.art: Two round dosas side by side on banana leaves, one cut into 3 equal pieces and one cut into 8 equal pieces, with one piece of each lifted out so the big piece and the small piece can be compared.

intro.hook: Which is more: half of a laddu, or a quarter of a laddu? Think first. Then open the box below.
intro.text: Someone offers you a choice. You can have one half of a laddu, or one quarter of a laddu. Which do you take? Now here is the catch. You have not seen the two laddus yet. One of them might be as small as a marble. The other might be as big as a coconut. Can you still choose? A fraction is a way to talk about equal parts of something. One half means the thing was cut into 2 equal parts, and you have one of them. One quarter means it was cut into 4 equal parts, and you have one. But a half of what? A quarter of what? In this lesson you will make your own fraction strips from paper and share out groundnuts. You will find a pattern that surprises most people the first time. Then you will use it in the kitchen, in music and in a game.
intro.art: A child looking at two closed steel boxes, one labelled 'one half of a laddu' and one labelled 'one quarter of a laddu', with a thought bubble holding a tiny laddu and a huge laddu.

outcomes: I can say what a fraction is: one or more equal parts of a whole.
I can name and write unit fractions: one half, one third, one quarter, one fifth, one sixth, one eighth and one tenth.
I can explain why more equal parts make each part smaller, so 1/8 of a thing is smaller than 1/3 of it.
I can find a unit fraction of a group by sharing it equally: one quarter of 12 is 3.
I can explain why a fraction has no size until I know what the whole is.
I can check that parts are equal in amount, even when they have different shapes.
I can point to what people chose about fractions: the whole, what counts as equal, and how to write them.

terms.meaning: All of the thing or the group you are sharing. It is what we agree to call 'one'.
terms.example: One dosa can be the whole. A bag of 12 groundnuts can also be the whole.
terms.art: A full round dosa next to a small heap of 12 groundnuts, each with a ring drawn round it and the label 'one whole'.

terms.meaning: Parts that are the same amount as each other. They do not have to be the same shape.
terms.example: A square sheet folded corner to corner gives 2 equal triangles. Folded edge to edge, it gives 2 equal rectangles.
terms.art: Two squares of paper, one folded into two triangles and one into two rectangles, with an equals sign between a triangle and a rectangle.

terms.meaning: A number that tells how much of a whole you have, counted in equal parts.
terms.example: If a chapati is cut into 4 equal parts and you eat 1 part, you ate the fraction one quarter.
terms.art: A chapati cut into 4 equal pieces with one piece on a small plate.

terms.meaning: One single equal part of a whole. When we write it, the top number is 1.
terms.example: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 and 1/8 are unit fractions. 3/4 is not, because it is three parts.
terms.art: A row of paper strips, each cut into a different number of equal parts, with just one part of each coloured in.

terms.meaning: One of 2 equal parts of a whole. We write it 1/2.
terms.example: Break a coconut into 2 equal parts. Each part is one half.
terms.art: A coconut broken into two equal halves.

terms.meaning: One of 3 equal parts of a whole. We write it 1/3.
terms.example: Three friends share one banana equally. Each gets one third.
terms.art: A banana cut into three equal lengths, one for each of three hands.

terms.meaning: One of 4 equal parts of a whole. It is also called a fourth. We write it 1/4.
terms.example: A quarter of an hour is 15 minutes, because 4 lots of 15 minutes make an hour.
terms.art: A clock face with the part from 12 to 3 shaded.

terms.meaning: One of 5, 6, 8 or 10 equal parts of a whole. We write them 1/5, 1/6, 1/8 and 1/10. The name comes from the number of equal parts.
terms.example: A tray holds 6 eggs. One egg is one sixth of the tray.
terms.art: An egg tray of 6 with one egg lifted out, labelled 1/6.

terms.meaning: The number written above the line in a fraction. It counts how many parts you have. Its proper name is the numerator.
terms.example: In 1/4 the top number is 1. You have one part.
terms.art: The fraction 1 over 4 written large, with an arrow to the 1 and the words 'parts you have'.

terms.meaning: The number written below the line in a fraction. It tells how many equal parts make the whole. Its proper name is the denominator.
terms.example: In 1/4 the bottom number is 4. Four equal parts make the whole.
terms.art: The fraction 1 over 4 written large, with an arrow to the 4 and the words 'equal parts in the whole'.

terms.meaning: A fraction can be taken of a group of things. Share the group into equal smaller groups. One of those groups is the unit fraction.
terms.example: Share 12 groundnuts into 4 equal groups. Each group has 3. So one quarter of 12 is 3.
terms.art: Twelve groundnuts arranged in 4 rings of 3, one ring coloured in.

terms.meaning: A drawing of a long box that stands for the whole. You split the box into equal parts to see a fraction.
terms.example: Draw a bar for 12. Split it into 4 equal boxes. Write 3 in each box.
terms.art: A long rectangle labelled 12 above, split into 4 equal boxes with a 3 inside each.

explanations.definition: A fraction tells how much of a whole you have, when the whole is split into equal parts.
explanations.description: To make a fraction you need three things. First, you need a whole: one dosa, one strip of paper, or one bag of 12 groundnuts. Second, you split the whole into parts that are equal. Third, you count how many of those parts you have. If the parts are not equal, there is no fraction to name. A dosa torn into one big piece and one small piece has two pieces, but neither piece is a half.
examples: A strip of paper folded end to end has 2 equal parts. Each part is one half of the strip.
A bar of chikki with 6 equal squares: one square is one sixth of the bar.
A dosa torn into a big piece and a small piece: 2 pieces, but no halves.
explanations.art: Three panels: a paper strip folded into two equal parts, a chikki bar of 6 equal squares with one broken off, and a dosa torn into one big and one small piece with a cross beside it.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the unit: what a fraction is, and why the parts must be equal.

explanations.concept: How to say and write a unit fraction
explanations.definition: A unit fraction is one equal part of a whole. It is written as 1, a short line, and the number of equal parts in the whole.
explanations.description: Count the equal parts in the whole. That number gives the fraction its name. Two parts give halves, 3 give thirds, 4 give quarters, 5 give fifths, 6 give sixths, 8 give eighths and 10 give tenths. On paper, write 1, draw a short line under it, and write the number of parts under the line. On a phone or in a book it is often written on one line, like this: 1/4. Here is a worked example. A strip is cut into 6 equal parts and you hold one. Count the parts: 6. So the name is one sixth. Write 1 on top, because you hold 1 part. Write 6 underneath, because 6 equal parts make the whole. You hold 1/6 of the strip.
examples: One of 3 equal parts: one third, written 1/3.
One of 8 equal parts: one eighth, written 1/8.
One of 10 equal parts: one tenth, written 1/10.
explanations.art: A paper strip split into 6 equal parts with one part shaded, and beside it the fraction written with 1 above a line and 6 below, with arrows: '1 part taken' and '6 equal parts in the whole'.
explanations.context: This card shows how to name a single equal part and how to write it with two numbers and a line.

explanations.concept: More equal parts means smaller parts
explanations.definition: When the same whole is cut into more equal parts, each part is smaller. So a bigger bottom number means a smaller unit fraction.
explanations.description: Take two strips of paper, each 24 cm long. Cut the first into 3 equal parts. Each part is 8 cm long. Cut the second into 8 equal parts. Each part is only 3 cm long. The strips were the same length, so the paper had to be shared among more parts, and each part got less. This is why 1/8 of a thing is smaller than 1/3 of the same thing, even though 8 is a bigger number than 3. The bottom number is not a size. It tells how many parts the whole was cut into. The same thing happens with people. A dosa shared by 8 people gives each person less than the same dosa shared by 3.
examples: From the same strip: 1/2 is longer than 1/3, 1/3 is longer than 1/4, and 1/4 is longer than 1/8.
One laddu shared by 2 children gives bigger pieces than one laddu shared by 10 children.
This rule only works when the whole is the same. See the card 'The whole decides the size'.
explanations.art: Five strips of the same length stacked under each other, cut into 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 equal parts, with one part of each shaded so the shaded parts get shorter going down the stack.
explanations.context: This card explains what you found with the paper strips: why one eighth of a strip is smaller than one third of the same strip.

explanations.definition: To find a unit fraction of a group, share the group into that many equal smaller groups. The number in one small group is the answer.
explanations.description: A whole does not have to be one thing. It can be a group, such as 12 groundnuts. Here is a worked example: find one quarter of 12. The bottom number is 4, so share the 12 into 4 equal groups. Put one groundnut in each group, then another in each, until they are all used. Each group has 3. So one quarter of 12 is 3. You can draw this as a bar model. Draw a long box for the 12. Split it into 4 equal boxes. The 12 is shared equally, so each box holds 3. Sharing into equal groups is division. So one quarter of 12 is the same sum as 12 divided by 4.
examples: One half of 12 is 6, because 12 shared into 2 equal groups gives 6 in each.
One third of 12 is 4, because 12 shared into 3 equal groups gives 4 in each.
One fifth of 20 rupees is 4 rupees, because 20 shared into 5 equal groups gives 4 in each.
explanations.art: Twelve groundnuts in 4 rings of 3 with one ring shaded, and under it a bar model: a long box labelled 12 split into four boxes, each with 3 written inside.
explanations.context: This card shows how to find a fraction of a group of things, such as one quarter of 12 groundnuts, with a worked example.

explanations.definition: A fraction tells how many equal parts the whole was cut into. How much you really get depends on how big the whole is.
explanations.description: One quarter of 24 groundnuts is 6 groundnuts. One quarter of 12 groundnuts is 3 groundnuts. Both are one quarter, and they are different amounts. The fraction stayed the same and the whole changed. So you cannot say that one half is always more than one quarter. One half of 8 laddus is 4 laddus. One quarter of 40 laddus is 10 laddus. Here the quarter is more. You can only compare two fractions by their bottom numbers when both are fractions of the same whole. This is why, when someone says 'half price' or 'a quarter of the class', a careful person asks: half of what? A quarter of how many?
examples: A quarter of a kilogram of tomatoes is 250 grams. A quarter of 100 grams of pepper is only 25 grams.
Half of a small dosa can be less food than a quarter of a very big dosa.
One tenth of 100 rupees is 10 rupees. One half of 10 rupees is 5 rupees.
explanations.art: Two bar models under each other: a long bar labelled 24 with one of its four parts shaded and marked 6, and a bar half as long labelled 12 with one of its four parts shaded and marked 3.
explanations.context: This card explains why the same fraction, such as one quarter, can be a different amount each time.

explanations.concept: Equal means the same amount, not the same shape
explanations.definition: The parts of a fraction must be equal in amount. They do not have to look the same, and they do not have to be the same height.
explanations.description: Fold one square of paper into 4 long strips. Fold another square of the same size into 4 small squares. Fold a third along both corner-to-corner lines, to make 4 triangles. A strip, a small square and a triangle look different. But each is one quarter of the same square, so each is the same amount of paper. You can check. Cut the triangle into two pieces, and the pieces fit exactly on top of the small square. The opposite mistake also happens: parts can look equal and not be. Water in a kadai is a good example. A kadai is narrow at the bottom and wide at the top. So the bottom half of its height holds much less than half of the water.
examples: Four triangles made by folding a square corner to corner, both ways, are four quarters.
Three lines drawn side by side across a circle do not make quarters. The two middle pieces are bigger than the two end pieces.
In a straight-sided glass, a quarter of the height is a quarter of the water. In a kadai it is not.
explanations.art: Three same-size squares split into quarters in three ways (4 strips, 4 small squares, 4 triangles), with one quarter of each shaded, and beside them a circle cut by three side-by-side lines with a cross beside it.
explanations.context: This card explains what 'equal parts' really means. It uses folded paper squares, and water poured into a kadai, which is a round-bottomed cooking pan.

explanations.concept: More than one part: a first look
explanations.definition: Fractions can count more than one equal part. Three quarters, written 3/4, means 3 parts when the whole is cut into 4 equal parts.
explanations.description: Unit fractions are the building blocks of all other fractions. If one quarter of a dosa is one part, then two quarters are two of those parts and three quarters are three of them. The top number counts the parts. The bottom number still says how many equal parts make the whole. Here is a worked example with a group. Find three quarters of 12. First find one quarter: 12 shared into 4 equal groups gives 3. Three quarters is three of those groups: 3 and 3 and 3, which is 9. You will do much more with fractions like these in the next level. This card is only a first look.
examples: Two thirds of a strip, written 2/3, is 2 parts when the strip is cut into 3 equal parts.
Four quarters, written 4/4, is all 4 parts. That is the whole.
Three quarters of 12 groundnuts is 9 groundnuts.
explanations.art: A strip cut into 4 equal parts with 3 parts shaded and labelled 3/4, above a row of 12 groundnuts in 4 groups of 3 with three groups ringed.
explanations.context: This card looks ahead. So far every fraction has been one single part. Here you see what happens when you take more than one part.

explanations.concept: People wrote fractions in different ways
explanations.definition: The way we write a fraction, with one number above a line and one below, is a choice people made. Other people made other choices that worked too.
explanations.description: About 3,500 years ago in Egypt, scribes wrote almost every fraction as a unit fraction. They had a special sign for two thirds. For three quarters they wrote one half and one quarter. In India, mathematicians wrote one number above the other, with any number on top. Brahmagupta did this in the year 628. Arab mathematicians later added the line between the two numbers. Old Tamil accounts had their own names for small parts: arai for one half, kaal for one quarter, araikkaal for one eighth, maa for one twentieth and kaani for one eightieth. Another, mundiri, was 1 part in 320. Until 1957, the Indian rupee was split into 16 annas, so 'four annas' meant a quarter of a rupee. Today a rupee is split into 100 paise. None of these ways is wrong. Each one is a different way to cut up and name the same whole.
examples: Egyptian scribes wrote three quarters as 1/2 and 1/4 together.
In a Tamil Nadu market you still hear 'kaal kilo' for a quarter of a kilogram and 'arai kilo' for half.
A rupee was once 16 annas and is now 100 paise. The rupee is the same whole, cut differently.
explanations.art: A row of four small panels: an Egyptian scribe's reed pen and papyrus, a palm-leaf page with two numbers one above the other and no line, a paper with a modern fraction 1 over 4, and old anna coins beside a modern rupee.
explanations.context: This card is about the human side of fractions: the different ways people in Egypt, India and elsewhere chose to write and name parts of a whole.

explanations.concept: Fractions in the sky, the Earth and the day
explanations.definition: People use fractions to describe the world around them. Each time, someone first chose what to call the whole.
explanations.description: The Earth turns round once, and we call that one day. Long ago, people in Egypt counted 12 hours of daylight and 12 hours of night. Our 24 hours come from that count. Timekeepers in India cut the same day into 60 parts. In Tamil each part is called a nazhigai, and it lasts 24 minutes. The day is the same. The cutting was a choice. The Moon gives another example. When the Moon looks like a half circle, astronomers call it a quarter Moon. The quarter is not a quarter of the Moon's face. The Moon has gone one quarter of the way round the Earth. So the same Moon is a half or a quarter, depending on which whole you mean. About one fifth of the air you breathe is oxygen. A little less than three quarters of the Earth's surface is covered by water.
examples: One hour is one twenty-fourth of a day. One nazhigai is one sixtieth of a day.
A first quarter Moon looks half lit. The Moon is one quarter of the way round the Earth.
If you sleep 8 hours, you sleep for one third of the day.
explanations.art: A split picture: the Earth with a ring round it cut into 24 parts on one side and 60 parts on the other, and a half-lit Moon one quarter of the way along a circle drawn round the Earth.
explanations.context: This card links fractions to the day, the Moon, the air and the sea. It shows that the same thing can be a different fraction when you pick a different whole.

explanations.concept: Other animals and parts of a whole
explanations.description: Humans are not the only animals who can tell one part of a whole from another. In 1981, two scientists in the United States, Guy Woodruff and David Premack, tested a chimpanzee called Sarah. She was shown something like a jar half full of liquid. She then had to pick what matched it, such as half of a wooden disc or three quarters of a disc. Sarah picked the matching fraction far more often than chance would allow. Four younger chimpanzees in the same study did not manage it. In 2016, Rosa Rugani and her team in Italy trained chicks who were four days old. The chicks learned to choose pictures that showed a proportion of 4 to 1, and not pictures that showed 2 to 1. When the pictures were changed to new amounts, the chicks still chose the 4 to 1 proportion. So these animals can respond to how much of a whole there is. What it is like for them, and whether they think of a half the way we do, nobody knows.
examples: Sarah the chimpanzee matched a half-full jar with half a disc, not with three quarters of a disc.
Four-day-old chicks chose the same proportion even when the amounts in the pictures changed.
A lady's finger cut across usually shows 5 nearly equal chambers. A star fruit usually has 5 ridges.
explanations.art: A chimpanzee looking at a half-full jar and pointing at half a wooden disc, and beside her three young chicks walking towards one of two picture cards.
explanations.context: This card is about fractions in other living beings. It tells what two real studies found with a chimpanzee and with chicks, and what is still not known.

explanations.concept: Can you halve something for ever?
explanations.description: Fold a strip in half, then in half again, and again. The parts go 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16. With numbers, this never has to stop. Any number can be halved, and the answer can be halved again. With real things it is different, and people give different answers.
examples: A sheet of newspaper can be folded in half only about 6 or 7 times before it is too thick to fold.
Half of 1 is 1/2, half of that is 1/4, then 1/8, then 1/16, and the list has no end.

perspectives.explanation: In numbers, yes. However small a fraction is, half of it is another fraction. There is no smallest fraction. Hui Shi, a thinker in China about 2,300 years ago, said the same about a stick: take half each day and it is never used up.

With real stuff, no. Keep cutting a grain of jaggery and you reach single sugar molecules. Cut a molecule and the pieces are no longer sugar. So a real thing can be halved many times, but not for ever and stay the same stuff.
Nobody knows whether space can be halved for ever. Some physicists think there may be a smallest possible length. No experiment has settled it.

explanations.art: A paper strip being cut in half again and again, the pieces getting smaller towards the right, ending in a magnifying glass over a dot with a question mark.
explanations.context: This card asks how far halving can go. The answer is different for numbers and for real things.

agreed.text: A fraction needs a whole and equal parts.
agreed.evidence: If the parts are unequal, two people can each hold 'one of 4 pieces' and have different amounts. Then the name tells you nothing. You saw this with the circle cut by three side-by-side lines.

agreed.text: From the same whole, more equal parts means smaller parts.
agreed.evidence: Your 24 cm strips show it. Two parts are 12 cm each, 3 parts are 8 cm each, 4 parts are 6 cm, 6 parts are 4 cm and 8 parts are 3 cm. The length of one part times the number of parts is always 24.

agreed.text: A unit fraction of a group is found by equal sharing, which is division.
agreed.evidence: Share 24 groundnuts into 4 equal groups and each group has 6. Whoever does the sharing, and in whatever order, the answer is 6.

agreed.text: The same fraction of different wholes gives different amounts.
agreed.evidence: One quarter of 24 groundnuts is 6. One quarter of 12 groundnuts is 3.

agreed.text: Once people agree on the whole and on what equal means, everyone gets the same answer.
agreed.evidence: Egyptian scribes, Indian mathematicians and children today write fractions differently. All of them find that two quarters of a thing make one half of it.

challenging.claim: One eighth is bigger than one third, because 8 is bigger than 3.
challenging.who: Many children, and many adults too, the first time they meet fractions
challenging.for: With whole numbers, 8 really is more than 3. It feels natural to read the bottom number as a size.
challenging.against: The bottom number counts how many parts the whole was cut into. Cut a 24 cm strip into 8 parts and each is 3 cm. Cut it into 3 parts and each is 8 cm. More parts means smaller parts.
challenging.context: This card looks at the most common mistake with fractions: reading the bottom number as if it were a size.

challenging.claim: A fraction is not really a number. Only whole numbers are numbers.
challenging.who: Greek mathematicians such as Euclid, about 2,300 years ago
challenging.for: Euclid said a number is a collection of ones. If the one is the smallest thing you count with, it cannot be broken.
challenging.against: Fractions can be added, compared, put in order and placed on a number line, just like whole numbers. Mathematicians in India worked with them as numbers. In 1585 Simon Stevin argued that every quantity is a number, and that is the view used today. It was a change in what people agreed to call a number.
challenging.context: This card is about an old view of what counts as a number, and why people gave it up.

challenging.claim: Fractions were there before people. People only discovered them.
challenging.who: Many mathematicians and philosophers, often called Platonists after the Greek thinker Plato
challenging.for: A chimpanzee and a chick can respond to a half or to a proportion without any human words. Two quarters make a half whoever does the sum, in any country and any century.
challenging.against: The whole, the meaning of 'equal' and the way of writing all have to be chosen before any fraction exists. Egyptians, Tamil accountants and modern schools chose differently. Mathematics is a language people made, and its sentences are true inside the rules people chose.
challenging.context: This card is about a big disagreement: are fractions something people made, or something people found?

challenging.claim: Sharing equally is always the fair way to share.
challenging.for: Equal parts are simple, anyone can check them, and nobody can say they were cheated.
challenging.against: Mathematics can tell you whether parts are equal. It cannot tell you whether equal is fair. A baby and a farmer who has worked all day may not need the same share of rice. 'Fair' is something people decide. 'Equal' is something you can measure.
challenging.context: This card is about the words 'equal share' and 'fair share'. They are often used as if they mean the same thing.

challenging.claim: There is one right way to cut a thing into quarters.
challenging.for: Most pictures in books show a circle cut like a cross, or a bar cut into 4 boxes.
challenging.against: A square can be cut into 4 strips, 4 small squares, 4 triangles and many other shapes. Each is a quarter as long as the 4 parts are the same amount.
challenging.context: This card is about whether quarters must always look the same.

big_questions.q: Why is one eighth of a dosa smaller than one third of it, when 8 is bigger than 3?
big_questions.hint: Think about how many people are sharing the dosa each time.

big_questions.q: Can a half ever be smaller than a quarter?
big_questions.hint: A half of what? A quarter of what? Try a small laddu and a huge one.

big_questions.q: If you keep cutting a piece of paper in half, will you ever have nothing left?
big_questions.hint: Each cut leaves half of what was there. Is half of something ever nothing?

big_questions.q: Are two halves of a dosa still one dosa? What changed and what did not?
big_questions.hint: Count the pieces. Then think about how much dosa there is.

big_questions.q: Ten guavas are big and small. Is a fair half 5 guavas each, or the same weight each?
big_questions.hint: Both are 'equal', measured in two ways. Who decides which way to measure?

big_questions.q: Who decided that a day has 24 hours? Could it have been 10 or 60?
big_questions.hint: In Egypt people counted 12 hours for the day and 12 for the night. In India people also used 60 parts called nazhigai.

big_questions.q: You are one whole person and also one small part of your family. Which is the real 'one'?
big_questions.hint: The same thing can be a whole or a part. It depends on what you choose to look at.

big_questions.q: A chick can pick out a proportion. Does the chick know fractions?
big_questions.hint: What does it mean to know something if you have no word for it?

big_questions.q: Is sharing equally always sharing fairly?
big_questions.hint: Think of sharing food between a baby and a grown-up who is very hungry.

story.title: Half of What Is Left
story.note: Kuttanad is a real place in Kerala where the fields lie below the level of the sea and people travel by canal. Devu, Appu, Ammachi and the shop boat are made up.
text: In Kuttanad, in Kerala, the fields lie lower than the sea, and the houses stand in a row along the canals. Devu's house had a canal where other houses have a road. The shop came by boat. Every Tuesday and every Friday a long black boat came down the canal with rice, soap, matches and jaggery under a blue plastic sheet, and the woman who rowed it rang a cycle bell tied to the front.

That June the rain came early and did not stop. The canal rose over its bank and over the path beside it. It rose up the first step of the house and stopped at the second. The shop boat did not come on Friday. It did not come on Tuesday. 'When the water goes down,' the neighbours called across to each other, and nobody could say when that would be.

There was rice in the bin, and Ammachi, Devu's grandmother, caught fish from the back step. But there was only one block of jaggery in the tin. It was dark brown and no bigger than her little brother Appu's fist. Jaggery was for the evening coffee. Without it the coffee was black and bitter, and Appu, who was five, made a face like a squeezed lime.

Ammachi put the block on the wooden board. 'We do not know how many evenings the boat will stay away,' she said. 'So this is the rule. Each evening we use half of what is left. Only half.' She pressed the big knife down through the middle. One half went into the pot. The other half went back into the tin.

That evening the coffee was so sweet it was nearly payasam. Devu lay awake afterwards, thinking about the rule. Half of what is left. Tomorrow, half of the half. Then half of that. 'Appu,' she whispered, 'it will never finish. There is always a half left to cut.' Appu was pleased. He fell asleep believing in jaggery for ever.

On the second evening Ammachi cut the half in half. Devu looked at the piece that went into the pot. 'That is one quarter of the block we began with,' she said. The coffee was sweet enough. But the piece that went back into the tin was the same size as the piece in the pot, and Devu did not like how small it looked.

In the morning she took a piece of charcoal from the stove and drew a long box on the dry top step. That was the whole block. She drew a line down the middle and rubbed out one side. First evening, one half. She cut the side that was left in two. Second evening, one quarter. Then she kept going. The third evening would get one eighth. The fourth would get one sixteenth, a piece like a tamarind seed. The fifth would get a crumb.

'Ammachi is right,' she told Appu. 'It never finishes.' She looked at her drawing again. 'And after tomorrow it is never enough.' The first evening had eaten half of everything. The fifth evening would get a piece too small to taste. The rule looked after the block. It did not look after the evenings.

She took the drawing to Ammachi, who looked at it for a long time. 'Then tell me how many evenings,' Ammachi said. 'If I knew it was four, I would cut four equal pieces. If I knew it was ten, I would cut ten. To make equal parts, child, you must first know how many parts. I do not know. So I halve.'

Devu went back to the step and sat with her chin on her knees. How many evenings? Then she saw the jetty post. On the day the path went under, she had tied a red thread round the post at the top of the water, to see what the water would do. The thread was dry now. She measured down from it with her hand. The water had dropped one hand in two days. She pushed a stick down beside the path. The path was still two hands under. One hand in two days. Two hands. 'Four days,' she said out loud. 'Four more evenings, if the water keeps going the way it is going.'

Ammachi came and measured with her own hand, which was bigger, and got her own answer, which was nearly the same. She looked at the sky. 'The water has not read your thread,' she said. But she fetched the tin.

She put the last piece on the board, the quarter of the old block. It was the whole of what they had now. Devu held her breath. Ammachi did not cut it into four. She cut it into five. 'Four for your four evenings,' she said. 'And one for the evening the water makes a fool of you.' Five equal pieces lay in a row, each a little smaller than a fourth would have been. Devu worked it out on the step. Each piece was one fifth of what was left. It was one twentieth of the block they had started with.

For four evenings the coffee was the same: not very sweet, but sweet, and the same for each evening. Appu stopped making the lime face on the second day. On the fourth morning the path was still under a finger of water. Devu said nothing. Ammachi said nothing either, but she tapped the tin.
On the fifth evening the last piece went into the pot. They were drinking the coffee on the step when they heard it, far down the canal, coming closer: a cycle bell.
story.epiphany: For the parent: there are two honest ways to share out something when you cannot get more. Halving what is left never runs out, but each share is half the one before: one half, one quarter, one eighth. Equal parts give every evening the same amount, but you can only cut equal parts when you know how many parts you need. Devu finds the number by measuring the water, and Ammachi cuts five parts, not four, to be safe. Five parts are each a little smaller than four parts would be. The 'whole' also changes in the story. The quarter that is left becomes the new whole, and one fifth of it is one twentieth of the first block.
ask: Ammachi's rule was 'half of what is left'. What was good about that rule, and what went wrong with it?
Why could Ammachi not cut equal pieces until Devu had measured the water?
Ammachi cut five pieces and not four. Each piece was smaller. Was that a good choice? What would you have done?
