games.title: Bigger Share
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent, or with friends
games.context: This is a card game for 1 to 4 players. Each card shows a fraction of a group, such as '1/4 of 20'. You work out how many that is, and the bigger amount wins. You find out that a half does not always beat a quarter.

printables.title: 32 fraction cards, with the answer on the back

rules: Cut out the 32 cards. Shuffle them. Deal them out equally, so each player has a pile with the fraction side up. Do not look at the backs.
Each player reads the top card of their own pile out loud, for example 'one quarter of 20'.
Each player says how many their card is worth. Use seeds or draw a bar if you need to. Then turn the card over to check.
The player whose card is worth the most takes all the cards from that round and puts them in a winnings pile.
If two players tie for the most, each of them keeps their own card.
A player who said the wrong number before checking cannot win that round. Their card goes to the best of the other players.
Play until the piles are used up. The player with the most cards in their winnings pile wins.
Playing alone: lay out two cards. Say which is worth more before you check. Score 1 point each time you are right. There are 16 pairs, so try to beat your last score out of 16.

setup.art: Two small piles of paper cards on a floor mat, the top card of one showing '1/4 of 20' and the other '1/2 of 6', with a bowl of tamarind seeds beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Deal the cards with the fraction side up. Keep some seeds nearby.

setup.art: A child sharing 20 seeds into 4 equal groups of 5 beside a card that says '1/4 of 20'.
setup.caption: 2. Read your top card. Work out how many it is worth.

setup.art: Two cards turned over showing 5 and 3, and a child taking both cards.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the cards over to check. The bigger amount takes the cards.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 32 cards. 2. Put about 50 seeds or beans in a bowl for working things out. 3. Shuffle and deal the cards, fraction side up.
flow.say: Each card asks for a fraction of a group. The back tells how many that is. We work it out first, and then we check the back.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Deal them with the fraction side up. Do not peek at the backs. Keep a bowl of seeds nearby.
flow.context: This is the first step of the card game Bigger Share. Each card shows a fraction of a group, such as '1/4 of 20'. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Play one practice round together with the cards '1/2 of 10' and '1/5 of 20'. Share out seeds for each card. It does not count.
flow.say: Let's practise. This card says one half of 10. This one says one fifth of 20. Which do you think is worth more? Why?
flow.kid: Practise first. One card says one half of 10. The other says one fifth of 20. Which is worth more? Share out seeds to check.

ask.q: How did you find one fifth of 20?
good: I shared 20 into 5 equal groups and counted one group.
20 divided by 5 is 4.

check.q: Which is worth more: one half of 10 or one fifth of 20?
check.why: One half of 10 is 5, because 10 shared into 2 equal groups gives 5 each. One fifth of 20 is 4, because 20 shared into 5 equal groups gives 4 each. 5 is more than 4. Picking 'one fifth of 20' usually means looking only at the 20 and not sharing it out.

flow.context: This is the practice round of the card game Bigger Share. Each card shows a fraction of a group, and the card worth the most wins.

flow.do: Play the game through. Let your child share out seeds whenever they want to. Take your own turns honestly, and say your working out loud.
flow.say: Read your card. Tell me how many it is worth. Then turn it over and check.
flow.kid: Read your top card out loud. Say how many it is worth. Turn it over and check. The bigger number takes the cards.
flow.parent: After a few rounds many children stop using seeds for halves and quarters. Let that happen by itself. If a card is too hard, draw a bar, split it into equal boxes and fill in the boxes together.
flow.context: This is the main part of the card game Bigger Share. Players read a card such as '1/3 of 12', work out how many it is worth, and the bigger amount wins.

flow.do: Lay out the cards '1/2 of 4' and '1/8 of 40' side by side. Talk about which won more often in the game: cards with halves, or cards with big groups.
flow.say: Did the half cards always win? Look at these two. Which is worth more? What decides it?
flow.kid: Look at two cards. One says one half of 4. The other says one eighth of 40. Which is worth more? Why?

ask.q: Why can one eighth beat one half?
good: Because it is one eighth of a much bigger group.
The whole is different, so you cannot just compare the fractions.

check.q: Which is worth more: one half of 4 or one eighth of 40?
check.why: One half of 4 is 2. One eighth of 40 is 5, because 40 shared into 8 equal groups gives 5 each. A half is a bigger fraction than an eighth only when both come from the same whole. Here the wholes are 4 and 40. Picking 'one half of 4' usually means comparing the fractions and forgetting the wholes.

flow.context: This is the last step of the card game Bigger Share. You look back at the game and ask whether a half always beats a smaller fraction.

games.title: Small Number, Big Share
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent, or with friends
games.context: This is a dice game for 1 to 4 players with 12 seeds. The number you roll tells you how many equal groups to share the 12 seeds into. You score one group. You find out which rolls give big shares.

printables.title: 6 roll squares
items: Roll 1: share the 12 into 12 equal groups. Score one twelfth of 12.
Roll 2: share the 12 into 2 equal groups. Score one half of 12.
Roll 3: share the 12 into 3 equal groups. Score one third of 12.
Roll 4: share the 12 into 4 equal groups. Score one quarter of 12.
Roll 5: try to share the 12 into 5 equal groups. If you cannot, score nothing.
Roll 6: share the 12 into 6 equal groups. Score one sixth of 12.

rules: Put 12 seeds in a row in the middle. These 12 seeds are the whole. They stay there for the whole game.
On your turn, roll one dice. Find your roll on the board.
Share the 12 seeds into that many equal groups. Count the seeds in one group. That is your score for this turn.
Write your score on the score sheet and add it to your total. Push the seeds back into a row for the next player.
If the seeds cannot be shared equally with none left over, you score nothing on that turn.
The first player to reach 20 or more wins. If you play alone, count how many rolls you need to reach 20. Then try to beat that.
Second game: use 24 seeds as the whole, and play to 40.

setup.art: Twelve tamarind seeds in a row on a floor mat with one dice and a paper board of six squares beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Put 12 seeds in a row. They are the whole.

setup.art: A dice showing 4 and the 12 seeds shared into 4 equal groups of 3, with a child pointing at one group.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the dice. Share the 12 into that many equal groups.

setup.art: A hand writing the number 3 on a score sheet beside the fraction 1/4.
setup.caption: 3. Count one group. That is your score. Write it down.

flow.do: 1. Put 12 seeds or beans in a row. 2. Put the board and one dice beside them. 3. Give each player a column on the score sheet.
flow.say: These 12 seeds are our whole. The dice tells us how many equal groups to make. Your score is one group.
flow.kid: Put 12 seeds in a row. They are the whole. Get one dice and the score sheet.

ask.q: Before we play: which roll do you hope for, a big number or a small one? Why?
good: Any guess with a reason. Do not correct it yet.

flow.context: This is the first step of the dice game Small Number, Big Share. You share 12 seeds into equal groups, and the dice tells you how many groups. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Take turns. Roll, share the 12 seeds into that many equal groups, count one group, and write the score. Play until someone reaches 20.
flow.say: Roll the dice. Share the 12 into that many equal groups. How many are in one group? What fraction of the 12 is that?
flow.kid: Roll the dice. Share the 12 seeds into that many equal groups. Count one group. Write your score.
flow.parent: The scores are 1, 6, 4, 3, 0 and 2 for rolls of 1 to 6. On a roll of 5, let your child try. They will get 5 groups of 2 with 2 seeds left over. Twelve cannot be shared into 5 equal groups of whole seeds. Do not tell them the scores. Let them find each one with the seeds.
flow.context: This is the main part of the dice game Small Number, Big Share. On each turn you roll a dice, share 12 seeds into that many equal groups, and score one group.

flow.do: Look at the score sheet together. Ask which roll gave the most seeds and which gave the fewest. Then ask about the roll of 1.
flow.say: Which roll was the best to get? Is that the roll you hoped for at the start? Why does a roll of 6 give so few?
flow.kid: Look at your scores. Which roll gave the most seeds? Which gave the fewest? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why does a 2 score more than a 6?
good: With 2 groups, each group gets more seeds.
Six groups have to share the same 12 seeds, so each group is small.

check.q: You share 12 seeds into equal groups and score one group. Which roll scores the most?
check.why: A roll of 2 makes 2 groups of 6, so you score 6. A roll of 4 gives 3, and a roll of 6 gives only 2. Fewer groups means more seeds in each group. Picking 'a roll of 6' usually means thinking a bigger number must give a bigger share.

flow.think: A roll of 1 made 12 groups and scored 1. What if a roll of 1 meant 'share into 1 group'? How much would you score then?
flow.context: This is the last step of the dice game Small Number, Big Share. You look at which rolls gave big shares of the 12 seeds and which gave small ones.

items.p: A dosa is cut into 4 pieces. When is one piece exactly one quarter?
opts: Only when the 4 pieces are equal
Only when the dosa is round
items.why: A quarter is one of 4 equal parts. If the pieces are unequal, there are 4 pieces but no quarters. Picking 'always' usually means counting pieces without checking that they are equal.
items.art: A dosa cut into 4 equal pieces next to a dosa cut into 4 unequal pieces.

items.p: A strip is cut into 6 equal parts. One part is one ____ of the strip.
items.why: The name comes from the number of equal parts. Six equal parts give sixths, so one part is one sixth, written 1/6.

items.p: Match each fraction name to the way it is written.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The top number is 1, because it is one part. The bottom number is the number of equal parts in the whole: 2 for halves, 3 for thirds, 4 for quarters, 8 for eighths and 10 for tenths.

items.p: In the fraction 1/5, what does the 5 tell you?
opts: The whole is cut into 5 equal parts
items.why: The bottom number tells how many equal parts make the whole. The top number, 1, tells how many parts you have. Picking 'you have 5 parts' mixes up the top and bottom numbers.

items.p: These are parts of the same strip. Put them in order, from the SHORTEST piece to the LONGEST.
items.a: order shown
items.why: More equal parts means shorter parts. The strip cut into 8 has the shortest pieces, then 6, then 4, then 3. The strip cut into 2 has the longest pieces.

items.p: One eighth of a chapati is bigger than one third of the same chapati.
items.why: False. A chapati cut into 8 equal parts has smaller parts than the same chapati cut into 3. Thinking it is true usually means reading the 8 as a size.

items.p: One half of 12 groundnuts is ____ groundnuts.
items.why: Share 12 into 2 equal groups. Each group has 6. So one half of 12 is 6.

items.p: One third of 12 groundnuts is ____ groundnuts.
items.why: Share 12 into 3 equal groups. Each group has 4. So one third of 12 is 4.

items.p: One quarter of 20 marbles is ____ marbles.
items.why: Share 20 into 4 equal groups. Each group has 5. So one quarter of 20 is 5.

items.p: How do you find one sixth of 18 bananas?
opts: Share 18 into 6 equal groups and count one group
items.why: The bottom number, 6, tells you how many equal groups to make. 18 shared into 6 equal groups gives 3 in each, so one sixth of 18 is 3. Picking 'take 6 away' treats the 6 as an amount to remove.

items.p: Sort these. Are the parts EQUAL or NOT EQUAL?
items: a square folded corner to corner
a circle cut by 3 lines side by side
a strip folded end to end
a banana cut into a long piece and a short piece
a rectangle folded in half twice
items.a: see items
items.why: Folding a shape so that one side lies exactly on the other makes equal parts. Lines side by side across a circle leave fat middle pieces and thin end pieces. Tearing and guessing do not give equal parts.

items.p: Draw a rectangle. Split it into 3 equal parts. Shade one part and write its fraction.
items.a: A rectangle with 2 lines that split it into 3 parts of the same size. One part is shaded. The label is 1/3 or 'one third'.
items.why: Three equal parts are thirds. One shaded part is one third. A strong drawing has parts that really look equal.

items.p: A friend says 1/8 is bigger than 1/3, because 8 is bigger than 3. What would you show her?
items.a: I would take two strips of the same length. I would cut one into 3 equal parts and one into 8 equal parts, and lay one piece of each side by side. The eighth is much shorter. The 8 means the strip was shared into more parts, so each part is smaller.
items.why: A strong answer shows it with the same whole cut two ways, and says what the bottom number counts.

items.p: A tray holds 6 eggs. What fraction of the tray is one egg?
items.why: The tray is the whole and it has 6 equal places. One egg is one of 6 equal parts, so it is 1/6. Picking 1/5 usually means counting only the other 5 eggs.

items.p: Draw 12 small circles for 12 laddus. Put a ring round one quarter of them.
items.a: 12 circles with a ring round 3 of them. A strong drawing first splits the 12 into 4 equal groups of 3.
items.why: One quarter of 12 is found by sharing 12 into 4 equal groups. Each group has 3.

items.p: Two quarters of the same square sheet must have the same shape.
items.why: False. A quarter can be a strip, a small square or a triangle. Quarters must be the same amount, not the same shape.

items.p: You are offered half of one dosa or a quarter of another dosa. Why can you not tell which is more?
items.a: Because I do not know how big each dosa is. Half of a small dosa can be less than a quarter of a very big dosa. A fraction only tells me how many equal parts there are, not how big the whole is.
items.why: A strong answer says that the two wholes may be different sizes, so the fractions alone cannot be compared.

worksheets.title: Fractions in the Market, the Clock and the Kitchen (stretch)

items.p: A kilogram is 1000 grams. One quarter of a kilogram is ____ grams.
items.why: Share 1000 into 4 equal parts. Half of 1000 is 500, and half of 500 is 250. In a Tamil Nadu market this is 'kaal kilo'.

items.p: A day has 24 hours. One third of a day is ____ hours.
items.why: Share 24 into 3 equal groups. Each group has 8. So one third of a day is 8 hours.

items.p: A rupee is 100 paise. Which coin was one quarter of a rupee?
items.why: 100 shared into 4 equal parts gives 25. So 25 paise is one quarter of a rupee. The 50 paise coin is one half of a rupee.

items.p: Which is more: one half of 6 or one quarter of 20?
items.why: One half of 6 is 3. One quarter of 20 is 5. The quarter is more here, because it is a quarter of a much bigger whole. Picking 'one half of 6' means comparing the fractions and forgetting the wholes.

items.p: One half is always more than one quarter, whatever the two wholes are.
items.why: False. One half of 8 is 4, but one quarter of 40 is 10. A half is more than a quarter only when both are fractions of the same whole.

items.p: Put these in order, from the SMALLEST amount to the BIGGEST.
items.a: order shown
items.why: Work each one out. One third of 9 is 3. One half of 8 is 4. One quarter of 20 is 5. One tenth of 60 is 6. The tenth is the biggest amount, because its whole is so big.

items.p: A bag has 30 tamarind seeds. Match each fraction of the bag to its number of seeds.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each time, share 30 into as many equal groups as the bottom number. More groups give fewer seeds in each group.

items.p: Adi tala has 8 beats. Its first section has 4 beats. What fraction of the cycle is that?
items.why: 8 beats split into 2 equal parts gives 4 beats in each part. So 4 beats is one half of the cycle. Picking 'one quarter' usually comes from seeing the number 4.
items.context: Adi tala is a cycle of 8 beats in South Indian classical music, kept by clapping and counting on the fingers.

items.p: A class of 24 children makes 4 equal teams. Each team is one ____ of the class.
items.why: The class is the whole. It is split into 4 equal parts, so each part is one quarter. Each team has 6 children.

items.p: One third of a string of beads is 5 beads. How many beads are on the whole string?
items.why: If one third is 5 beads, the whole string is 3 equal groups of 5. That is 15 beads. Picking 8 means adding 3 and 5. Here you go from the part back to the whole.

items.p: You have 12 murukkus. Explain how to find one third of them.
items.a: I share the 12 murukkus into 3 equal groups, giving one to each group in turn until they are used up. Each group has 4. One group is one third, so one third of 12 is 4.
items.why: A strong answer says to make 3 equal groups, because the bottom number is 3, and then counts one group.

items.p: Draw a bar for 20 rupees. Split it into 5 equal boxes. How many rupees go in each box?
items.a: A long box labelled 20, split into 5 equal boxes with 4 written in each. So one fifth of 20 rupees is 4 rupees.
items.why: The bar is the whole. Five equal boxes share the 20 rupees, so each holds 4. One box is one fifth.

items.p: Two children share a bag of 10 guavas. Some guavas are big and some are small.

views.says: Half means 5 guavas each. We count them out, one for you and one for me. That is equal.
Half means the same weight each. You have the 5 big ones. Your half is heavier than mine.

items.ask: Whose half is the real half? Pick a side and give your reason. Then say what the other child has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both children have shared equally, but by different measures. One counted guavas and the other compared weight. It picks one and gives a reason, such as 'by weight, because we eat the fruit, not the number'. It also says the other way is equal too, in its own measure. The two must agree what to measure before they share.
items.why: A fraction needs equal parts, and 'equal' needs a measure: number, weight, length or something else. People choose the measure. Once it is chosen, the sharing can be checked.

items.p: Four equal cups of water go into a round-bottomed kadai. After 1 cup, the water is half-way up. Why?
opts: The kadai is narrow at the bottom
The first cup had more water
Water shrinks as you add more
items.why: Each cup is the same amount. At the narrow bottom the water has little room to spread, so it stands tall. Higher up, the kadai is wide, and the same amount makes a thin layer.
items.context: A kadai is a cooking pan with a round bottom. In the experiment A Quarter of the Water, you pour 4 equal cups of water into one and measure the depth each time.

items.p: Two children each eat one quarter of their own chikki bar. One of them eats more chikki. How can that be?
items.a: Their chikki bars are different sizes. One quarter of a big bar is more chikki than one quarter of a small bar. The fraction is the same but the wholes are different.
items.why: A strong answer says that the two wholes are different, so the same fraction gives different amounts.

items.p: 12 beads can be shared into 5 equal groups with no beads left over.
items.why: False. Five groups of 2 use 10 beads and leave 2 over. 12 can be shared equally into 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12 groups, but not into 5.

items.p: A strip is cut into 4 equal parts, and 3 of them are shaded. What fraction is shaded?
items.why: The bottom number is the number of equal parts in the whole, which is 4. The top number is how many parts are shaded, which is 3. So it is 3/4, three quarters. Picking 4/3 puts the numbers the wrong way up.

items.p: One quarter of 12 beads is 3 beads. So three quarters of 12 beads is ____ beads.
items.why: Three quarters is 3 lots of one quarter. One quarter is 3 beads, so three quarters is 3 and 3 and 3, which is 9.

items.p: Fold a sheet of paper in half 3 times. Open it. It has ____ equal parts.
items.why: The first fold makes 2 parts. The second fold doubles them to 4. The third fold doubles them to 8. Each part is one eighth of the sheet.

items.p: What does each fold in half do to the parts of a sheet of paper?
opts: Twice as many parts, each half as big
Twice as many parts, each twice as big
One more part, each a bit smaller
items.why: Every part is folded in two, so the number of parts doubles and each part is half the size it was. The parts go 2, 4, 8, 16. Picking 'one more part' usually means adding when the parts are doubling.

items.p: Half of one half is one ____.
items.why: Cut a whole into 2 halves. Cut each half into 2 equal parts. Now there are 4 equal parts, so each is one quarter.

items.p: Two rotis are shared equally among 4 people. How much roti does each person get?
items.why: Cut each roti into 2 halves. That makes 4 halves, one for each person. Picking 'one quarter' usually means sharing only one of the rotis.

items.p: One half of a dosa and one quarter of the same dosa together make three quarters of it.
items.why: True. One half covers 2 quarters exactly. Add one more quarter and you have 3 quarters. Egyptian scribes wrote three quarters this way.

items.p: Work each one out. Then put them in order, from the LEAST to the MOST.
items.a: order shown
items.why: Work each one out. One half of 16 is 8. One third of 27 is 9. One tenth of 100 is 10. One quarter of 44 is 11. The smallest fraction here does not give the smallest amount.

items.p: One fifth of a number is 6. What is the number?
items.why: If one fifth is 6, the whole is 5 equal groups of 6. That is 30. Picking 11 means adding 5 and 6.

items.p: Can you cut a strip of paper in half for ever? Answer for real paper, and then for numbers.
items.a: With real paper, no. After about 10 cuts the piece is too small to hold or cut, and in the end you would reach the tiny particles the paper is made of. With numbers, yes. Half of 1/8 is 1/16, half of that is 1/32, and there is always another half.
items.why: A strong answer separates real things, which have a smallest piece you can cut, from numbers, which can always be halved again.

items.p: Draw a square. Shade one quarter of it in a shape that is not a square and not a straight strip.
items.a: One good answer is a triangle made by drawing both corner-to-corner lines and shading one of the 4 triangles. Other shapes work too, as long as the shaded part is exactly one of 4 equal amounts.
items.why: A quarter must be one of 4 equal amounts. It does not have to be any special shape.

items.p: A first quarter Moon looks half lit. What is the 'quarter' a quarter of?
opts: The Moon's trip round the Earth
items.why: Astronomers mean that the Moon has gone one quarter of the way round the Earth since the new Moon. The face we see is half lit. So the same Moon is a half or a quarter, depending on which whole you choose.
items.context: The Moon goes round the Earth about once a month. Part of the way round, we see it as a half circle of light, and astronomers call that a quarter Moon.

items.p: Match the number of equal parts to the name of one part.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The name of a unit fraction comes from the number of equal parts in the whole. This works for any number of parts, however many.

items.p: Two people argue about where fractions come from.

views.says: People made fractions up, like words. Egyptians wrote them one way and Indians another. We could have chosen differently.
Fractions were always there. Two quarters made a half before any person lived. A chick can pick out a proportion with no words at all.

items.ask: Who do you agree with more? Give a reason from something you did in this lesson. Then say what the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses evidence. For the first: we chose the whole each time, 24 groundnuts or 12, and we chose how to write 1/4. For the second: once the whole was chosen, one quarter of 24 was 6 whoever counted. It then says what the other side has right. Some children say both: the names and the wholes are chosen, and what follows is not.
items.why: This is a real disagreement among mathematicians and philosophers, and nobody has settled it. What matters is using evidence and answering the other side fairly.

items.p: Draw a strip in 4 equal parts. Shade one half red and one quarter blue. How much is shaded?
items.a: A strip of 4 equal boxes with 2 boxes red and 1 box blue. Three of the 4 boxes are shaded, so three quarters of the strip is shaded.
items.why: One half of the strip is 2 of the 4 boxes. One quarter is 1 box. Together they are 3 boxes out of 4, which is three quarters.

items.p: Sort these numbers of beads. Can they be shared into 3 equal groups with none left over?
items.a: see items
items.why: 9, 12 and 21 are in the 3 times table, so they share into 3 equal groups of 3, 4 and 7. With 10, 14 and 25 some beads are left over, so one third of them is not a whole number of beads.

items.p: 12 sweets share equally among 2, 3, 4 or 6 people. 10 share only among 2 or 5. Which is better?
items.a: 12 is better if I do not know how many people will share, because it can be shared equally among 2, 3, 4 or 6 people. 10 only works for 2 or 5 people. This may be why eggs and bangles are sold by the dozen, and why a day was cut into 24 hours.
items.why: A strong answer sees that a number with more ways to share equally is more useful for sharing. A child who picks 10 with a good reason, such as a family of 5, is also right.

experiments.title: The Strip Test: more parts, bigger or smaller?
experiments.context: This is the main investigation of the unit. You cut paper strips of the same length into 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 equal parts. Then you share 24 groundnuts into the same numbers of groups. You find out what happens to each part when there are more parts.
experiments.problem: A fraction is one or more equal parts of a whole. You will cut five strips that are all 24 cm long into different numbers of equal parts, and measure one part of each. Then you will do the same with 24 groundnuts.
experiments.question: When the same whole is cut into more equal parts, what happens to the size of each part?
experiments.predict: Before you cut anything, guess. Which will be longer: one third of a strip, or one eighth of the same strip? Say why you think so, and write your guess down.
experiments.fair_test: Every strip must start at exactly 24 cm, so that every strip is the same whole. The only thing you change is the number of equal parts. For the groundnuts, always start with all 24.
results_table: Length of one part of the strip (cm)

materials.item: strips of paper 24 cm long and about 3 cm wide, cut from newspaper or a used notebook page (one extra to keep whole)
a ruler marked in centimetres, a pencil and scissors
groundnuts in their shells, or rajma, tamarind seeds or buttons
a sheet of paper for the results table, and an envelope to keep the pieces

schedule.what: Guess first. Cut five strips into 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 equal parts and measure. Share 24 groundnuts the same way. Look for the pattern.

experiments.record: Fill in the table, one row for 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 parts. Then write one sentence that begins: 'When there are more equal parts, each part is…'

setup.art: Six paper strips of the same length lying in a row beside a ruler, each strip being marked with pencil lines at different equal spacings.
setup.caption: 1. Cut 6 strips, each 24 cm long. Mark them with a ruler.

setup.art: The strips cut into 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 equal pieces, with one piece of each lined up under an uncut whole strip, getting shorter down the page.
setup.caption: 2. Cut each strip into equal parts. Line up one part of each.

setup.art: Twenty-four groundnuts shared into 4 equal groups of 6 on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 3. Share 24 groundnuts into the same numbers of equal groups.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason before any cutting. Write the guess at the top of the results sheet. Do not say whether it is right.
flow.say: We will cut one strip into 3 equal parts and one into 8 equal parts. Which part will be longer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. One strip is cut into 3 equal parts. Another is cut into 8. Which part is longer? Say why. Write it down.

ask.q: Why do you think that one will be longer?
good: Any reason is fine at this stage.
Many children say 'an eighth, because 8 is more than 3'. Write it down and let the test answer it.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Strip Test. You will cut paper strips of the same length into different numbers of equal parts. Here you guess what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Cut 6 strips, each exactly 24 cm long. Keep one whole. 2. Mark the others with a ruler. For 2 parts, mark every 12 cm. For 3 parts, every 8 cm. For 4 parts, every 6 cm. For 6 parts, every 4 cm. For 8 parts, every 3 cm. 3. Cut along the marks.
flow.say: Each strip is the same whole. We cut this one into 2 equal parts, this one into 3, then 4, 6 and 8. Keep each strip's pieces together.
flow.kid: Cut 6 strips, each 24 cm long. Keep one whole. For 2 parts, mark at 12 cm. For 3 parts, mark every 8 cm. For 4 parts, every 6 cm. For 6 parts, every 4 cm. For 8 parts, every 3 cm. Cut on the marks. Keep each strip's pieces in its own heap.
flow.parent: Help with the measuring, since small errors spoil the result. A quick check: stack the pieces from one strip. They should match. Younger hands may need help cutting the 3 cm pieces.
flow.context: This is the second step of the Strip Test. You cut five paper strips, each 24 cm long, into 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 equal parts.

flow.do: 1. Lay the whole strip at the top. 2. Under it, lay one piece from each cut strip, in order from longest to shortest. 3. Measure each piece and fill in the table.
flow.say: Put one piece from each strip under the whole strip, longest first. Measure each one. What do you notice as the number of parts goes up?
flow.kid: Lay one piece from each strip under the whole strip. Put the longest first. Measure each piece. Write the lengths in your table. What do you notice?

ask.q: What happens to the pieces as the number of parts goes up?
good: They get shorter.
More parts, smaller parts.

ask.q: Was your guess right?
good: An honest look back at the guess, whichever way it went.

flow.parent: The lengths should be 12, 8, 6, 4 and 3 cm for 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 parts. Do not explain yet. Let your child say what they see first.

check.q: From strips of the same length, which piece is longer?
check.why: One third of a 24 cm strip is 8 cm. One eighth of the same strip is 3 cm. The strip cut into 8 has to share the same paper among more parts, so each part is smaller. Picking 'one eighth' usually means reading the 8 as a size. The 8 counts the parts.

flow.context: This is the third step of the Strip Test. You compare one piece from each of five paper strips that were cut into 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 equal parts.

flow.do: 1. Count out 24 groundnuts. 2. Share them into 2 equal groups and count one group. Write it in the table. 3. Do the same for 3, 4, 6 and 8 groups, starting with all 24 each time.
flow.say: Now the whole is 24 groundnuts. Share them into 2 equal groups. How many in one group? Now try 3 groups, then 4, 6 and 8.
flow.kid: Count out 24 groundnuts. Share them into 2 equal groups. Count one group and write it down. Now do 3 groups. Then 4, 6 and 8.

ask.q: Look at the two columns of numbers in your table. What do you notice?
good: They are the same numbers.
The centimetres and the groundnuts match, because both wholes are 24.

flow.parent: The groups should hold 12, 8, 6, 4 and 3 groundnuts. These match the strip lengths, because the strip was 24 cm and there are 24 groundnuts. Wait for your child to spot this.
flow.context: This is the fourth step of the Strip Test. After cutting 24 cm paper strips into equal parts, you now share 24 groundnuts into the same numbers of equal groups.

flow.do: 1. Put 12 of the groundnuts away. 2. Ask what one quarter of the 12 that are left will be. 3. Share them into 4 equal groups to check.
flow.say: One quarter of 24 was 6. Now there are only 12 groundnuts. What do you think one quarter of these will be? Why?
flow.kid: Put 12 groundnuts away. Now the whole is 12. Guess one quarter of 12. Then share them into 4 equal groups to check.

ask.q: One quarter was 6 before, and now it is 3. Why did it change?
good: The whole changed from 24 to 12.
A quarter of a smaller group is a smaller number.

check.q: One quarter of 24 groundnuts is 6. What is one quarter of 12 groundnuts?
check.why: Share 12 into 4 equal groups and each group has 3. The fraction is the same, one quarter, but the whole is smaller, so the amount is smaller. Picking 6 usually means thinking a fraction is a fixed amount. Picking 4 usually means mixing up the number of groups with the number in a group.

flow.context: This is the fifth step of the Strip Test. You have shared 24 groundnuts into equal groups. Now you change the whole to 12 groundnuts and see what happens to one quarter.

flow.do: Write the fraction on each paper piece: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/6 or 1/8. Fill in the last column of the table. Keep all the pieces in an envelope.
flow.say: Each piece has a name. This strip was cut into 6 equal parts, so each piece is one sixth. Write 1 above a line and 6 below it.
flow.kid: Write its fraction on every piece. One of 6 equal parts is one sixth. Write 1, a line, and 6 under it. Keep the pieces in an envelope.
flow.context: This is the sixth step of the Strip Test. You have cut paper strips into 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 equal parts. Now you write the fraction name on each piece.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences: what I think now, what I saw, and why I think it happens.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now about more parts? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happens?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What do I think now? What did I see? Why does it happen?
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: more equal parts means smaller parts. What I saw: one third of the strip was 8 cm and one eighth was 3 cm. Why: the strip is the same, so with more parts each part gets less of it.
flow.think: If you cut the 24 cm strip into 24 equal parts, how long would one part be? What about 48 parts?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Strip Test, where paper strips of the same length were cut into different numbers of equal parts. You say what you found and why.

experiments.title: A Quarter of the Water
experiments.context: In this experiment you pour 4 equal cups of water into a kadai, which is a round-bottomed cooking pan. You measure how deep the water is after the first cup and after the fourth. You find out whether a quarter of the water reaches a quarter of the way up.
experiments.problem: Equal parts must be equal in amount. With water, we often judge the amount by how high it stands. You will test whether that works in a pan with a round bottom and in a glass with straight sides.
experiments.question: Is one quarter of the water always one quarter of the height?
experiments.predict: You will pour 4 equal cups of water into a kadai, one after another. Before you start, guess. After the first cup, will the water be a quarter as deep as at the end, less than a quarter, or more? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same cup every time and fill it to the brim every time, so each cup is the same amount. Keep the pan flat on the table. Always measure in the middle, where the water is deepest.

materials.item: a small kadai or any pan or bowl with a round bottom
a glass or jar with straight sides, the same width from bottom to top
a small cup or tumbler for the kadai, and a much smaller measure for the glass, such as a bottle cap or a medicine cup (4 of them must fit)
a clean wooden stick, such as an ice-cream stick or a chopstick, a pen and a ruler
water, and a cloth for spills

schedule.what: Guess first. Pour 4 equal cups into a kadai and measure the depth after each. Do the same with a straight glass. Compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write: in which one was the first cup a quarter of the final depth?

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Your numbers depend on your pan and your cup.

setup.art: A small round-bottomed kadai on a table with a steel cup of water being poured into it and three more cups of water waiting.
setup.caption: 1. Pour 1 full cup into the kadai. It is one quarter of the water.

setup.art: A wooden stick held upright in the middle of the kadai, with a pen marking the wet line on the stick.
setup.caption: 2. Dip a stick in the middle. Mark how deep the water is.

setup.art: The same kadai after four cups, and beside it a straight-sided glass with four evenly spaced water marks.
setup.caption: 3. Pour 3 more cups, marking each time. Then try a straight glass.

flow.do: Show the empty kadai and the cup. Explain that 4 cups will go in. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write the guess down.
flow.say: Four equal cups will go in. So one cup is a quarter of the water. After one cup, how deep will it be, compared with the end? Why?
flow.kid: Four equal cups of water will go in the kadai. One cup is a quarter of the water. Will it reach a quarter of the way up? Guess, and say why.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Any reason. Many people say 'a quarter of the way up, because it is a quarter of the water'.

flow.context: This is the first step of the experiment A Quarter of the Water. You will pour 4 equal cups of water into a kadai, a round-bottomed pan. Here you guess what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Fill the cup to the brim and pour it into the kadai. 2. Hold the stick upright in the middle and mark the wet line with a pen. 3. Pour a second, third and fourth cup, marking the stick each time. 4. Measure the four marks with a ruler.
flow.say: Pour one full cup. Dip the stick straight down in the middle. Mark where the wet part ends. Now the next cup.
flow.kid: Fill the cup to the top. Pour it in the kadai. Dip the stick in the middle and mark the wet line. Do this 4 times. Measure the marks.
flow.parent: In a round-bottomed kadai the first cup often reaches about half of the final depth, and each new cup adds less height than the one before. If your pan has a flat bottom and sloping sides, the difference is small, only a few millimetres. A rounder bottom gives a clearer result.
flow.context: This is the second step of the experiment A Quarter of the Water. You pour 4 equal cups of water into a kadai, a round-bottomed pan, and mark the depth on a stick after each cup.

flow.do: 1. Dry the stick or turn it round. 2. Use the small measure and the straight glass. Pour in 4 equal measures, marking the depth after each. 3. Measure the marks.
flow.say: Now the same test in a glass with straight sides. Four equal measures. Mark the stick after each one. What do you see this time?
flow.kid: Now use the straight glass and the small measure. Pour in 4 equal measures. Mark the stick each time. Measure the marks.

ask.q: How are the marks different from the marks for the kadai?
good: They are evenly spaced.
Each measure lifts the water by the same amount.

flow.context: This is the third step of the experiment A Quarter of the Water. After pouring 4 equal cups into a round-bottomed kadai, you now pour 4 equal measures into a glass with straight sides.

flow.do: Put the two sets of marks side by side. Ask your child to explain the difference. Listen first, then look at the shapes of the kadai and the glass together.
flow.say: Each cup was the same amount of water. So why did the first cup stand so tall in the kadai? Look at its shape.
flow.kid: Look at both sets of marks. Each cup was the same amount. Why did the first cup stand taller in the kadai? Look at its shape.

ask.q: Why does the same amount of water stand taller at the bottom of the kadai?
good: The kadai is narrow at the bottom, so the water has less room to spread.
Higher up it is wide, so the same water makes a thin layer.

check.q: A kadai is narrow at the bottom and wide at the top. It is filled to half its height. How much of the water is in it?
options: Exactly half of a full kadai
Less than half of a full kadai
More than half of a full kadai
check.why: The bottom half of the height is the narrow part, so it holds less than the wide top half. Height shows the amount only when the sides are straight. Picking 'exactly half' usually means judging the amount by height alone.

flow.context: This is the fourth step of the experiment A Quarter of the Water. You compare how the water rose in a round-bottomed kadai and in a straight glass when equal cups were poured in.

flow.do: Ask for three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? Why does it happen?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What do I think now? What did I see? Why does it happen?
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a quarter of the water is not always a quarter of the height. What I saw: in the kadai the first cup came half-way up, and in the glass it came a quarter of the way up. Why: the kadai is narrow at the bottom.
flow.think: How could you mark a kadai so that the marks show true quarters of the water?
flow.context: This is the last step of the experiment A Quarter of the Water, in which equal cups of water were poured into a round-bottomed kadai and a straight glass. You say what you found.

activities.title: Fraction Hunt
activities.context: This is a hunt around your home for things that are already split into equal parts. A fraction is one or more equal parts of a whole. You find out how many fractions were in your home all along.
activities.problem: Many things at home come in equal parts: a strip of tablets, an egg tray, the panes of a window, the hours on a clock. For each one you will say what the whole is, how many equal parts it has, and what fraction one part is.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Find 8 things at home that are split into equal parts. Name the fraction for one part of each.

activities.record: Make a list of 8 things. For each, write the whole, the number of equal parts, and the fraction for one part.

setup.art: A child pointing at a window with 6 equal glass panes and a steel plate rack with 4 equal slots.
setup.caption: 1. Look for things made of equal parts.

setup.art: A notebook page with three columns headed 'The whole', 'Equal parts' and 'One part is', with 'egg tray, 6, 1/6' written in.
setup.caption: 2. Write the whole, the number of parts, and the fraction for one part.

setup.art: An orange opened into segments of slightly different sizes next to a bar of chocolate with equal squares.
setup.caption: 3. Check: are the parts really equal? If not, it is not a fraction.

flow.do: Explain the hunt and make three columns on the paper: the whole, the number of equal parts, and what one part is.
flow.say: Let's hunt for things that are already in equal parts. For each one, tell me the whole, and how many equal parts it has.
flow.kid: Hunt for things in equal parts. Find 8. For each, say the whole. Then count its equal parts.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Fraction Hunt. You look around your home for things that are split into equal parts.

flow.do: Walk round the home together. Look at windows, tiles, an egg tray, a strip of tablets, a clock, a calendar, a ludo board and an idli plate.
flow.say: Here is a strip of 10 tablets. What is the whole? What fraction is one tablet? Are all the parts equal?
flow.kid: Look at windows, tiles, trays, clocks and boards. Count the equal parts. One part of 10 equal parts is one tenth.
flow.parent: Good finds: one pane of a 6-pane window is one sixth. One tablet of a strip of 10 is one tenth. One day is one seventh of a week. One hour mark on a clock is one twelfth of the way round. Talk about things with unequal parts too, such as the segments of an orange. They are parts, but not a fraction you can name.

ask.q: The segments of an orange are not all the same size. Is one segment a fraction of the orange?
good: Not one we can name exactly, because the parts are not equal.
It is a part, but not one tenth or one eighth.

flow.context: This is the main step of the Fraction Hunt. You look around your home for things split into equal parts, and name the fraction for one part.

flow.do: Read the list back together. Ask which thing had the most equal parts and which had the fewest.
flow.say: Which of your finds had the most equal parts? Is one part of that a big fraction or a small one?
flow.kid: Read your list. Which thing has the most equal parts? Is one part of it big or small?

check.q: A week has 7 days. What fraction of a week is one day?
check.why: The week is the whole. It has 7 equal parts, the days. One of 7 equal parts is one seventh, written 1/7. Picking 'seven' usually means giving the number of parts and not the fraction.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Fraction Hunt, where you found things at home that are split into equal parts. You look back at your list.

activities.title: Neer Mor by Quarters
activities.context: This is a cooking activity. Neer mor is a thin, salted buttermilk drunk across South India in hot weather. You make it by measuring the curd and the water in quarters of a glass, and then you change the recipe and taste the difference.
activities.problem: Cooks use fractions all the time: half a cup, a quarter of a spoon. You will mark a straight glass in quarters with a folded paper strip. Then you will mix a drink that is one quarter curd and three quarters water.

materials.item: a glass or steel tumbler with straight sides
a strip of paper as tall as the glass, sticky tape, and a pen
fresh curd, about half a glass
drinking water, salt, and a jug or big bowl with a spoon or whisk
a few curry leaves, a small piece of ginger or a pinch of jeera powder, if you like them

schedule.what: Mark a glass in quarters. Make neer mor with one quarter curd and three quarters water. Try another recipe and compare the taste.

activities.record: Write your family's recipe as fractions of a glass: how much curd and how much water. Say which mix you liked best.

setup.art: A paper strip as tall as a straight glass, folded in half and in half again, then opened to show three fold lines.
setup.caption: 1. Fold a strip as tall as the glass in half, twice. Tape it on.

setup.art: A straight glass with a quartered paper strip taped up its side, curd filled up to the first fold line.
setup.caption: 2. Fill curd up to the first mark. That is one quarter of the glass.

setup.art: A child whisking curd and water in a steel jug, with a few curry leaves beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Add three quarters of a glass of water. Whisk with salt.

flow.do: 1. Cut a paper strip as tall as the glass. 2. Fold it in half, then in half again. Open it. 3. Tape it up the side of the glass. Draw a line on each fold.
flow.say: Fold the strip in half, and in half again. How many equal parts is it in now? Each part is one quarter of the glass.
flow.kid: Cut a strip as tall as the glass. Fold it in half. Fold it in half again. Open it and tape it on the glass.

ask.q: You folded in half twice. How many equal parts are there?
good: Four.
Half of a half is a quarter.

flow.parent: The glass must have straight sides. In a glass that is wider at the top, a quarter of the height is less than a quarter of the drink.
flow.context: This is the first step of making neer mor, a thin salted buttermilk. You mark a straight glass in quarters with a folded paper strip.

flow.do: 1. Spoon curd into the glass up to the first line. Tip it into the jug. 2. Fill the glass with water up to the third line. Tip it into the jug. 3. Add a pinch of salt and whisk.
flow.say: Fill curd to the first line. That is one quarter of a glass. Now water to the third line. That is three quarters. Whisk them together.
flow.kid: Fill curd up to the first line. Tip it in the jug. Fill water up to the third line. Tip it in. Add a pinch of salt and whisk.

ask.q: One quarter of curd and three quarters of water. How much drink is that altogether?
good: Four quarters, which is one whole glass.

flow.context: This is the second step of making neer mor, a thin salted buttermilk. You measure one quarter of a glass of curd and three quarters of a glass of water.

flow.do: 1. Pour out a little to taste. 2. Make a second mix: curd to the second line, and water to the second line. 3. Taste both. Add crushed curry leaves or ginger to the one you like.
flow.say: Now try half curd and half water. Which one do you like more? Which is thicker? Why?
flow.kid: Taste your neer mor. Now make another: half a glass of curd, half a glass of water. Taste both. Which do you like?

ask.q: Why is the second drink thicker?
good: It has a bigger fraction of curd.
Half is more than a quarter of the same glass.

flow.context: This is the third step of making neer mor, a thin salted buttermilk. You compare a drink that is one quarter curd with a drink that is half curd.

flow.do: Decide on the family recipe together. Write it down as fractions of a glass.
flow.say: Which recipe shall we keep? Write it as fractions. How much curd, and how much water?
flow.kid: Choose your best recipe. Write it down as fractions of a glass. How much curd? How much water?

check.q: A glass is one quarter curd. The rest is water. What fraction of the glass is water?
check.why: The glass has 4 quarters. One is curd, so 3 are water. Three quarters is written 3/4. Picking 'one quarter' usually means naming the curd again.

flow.context: This is the last step of making neer mor, a thin salted buttermilk made from measured quarters of a glass of curd and water. You write down your recipe.

activities.title: Clap Adi Tala in Halves and Quarters
activities.context: This is a music activity. A tala is a cycle of beats in South Indian classical music, kept with the hands. Adi tala has 8 beats. You clap it, and find the half, the quarters and the eighths inside it.
activities.problem: Musicians and dancers count time in equal parts. Adi tala, the most common tala in Carnatic music, has 8 beats in three sections: 4 beats, then 2 beats, then 2 beats. You will find what fraction of the cycle each section is.

materials.item: your hands, and a strip of paper with 8 equal boxes drawn on it

schedule.what: Learn to keep Adi tala with claps, finger counts and waves. Find the fractions in the 8 beats.

activities.record: Draw a strip of 8 boxes. Colour the first 4 boxes one colour, the next 2 another, and the last 2 a third. Write the fraction under each section.

setup.art: A child sitting cross-legged, clapping the right palm down on the right thigh.
setup.caption: 1. Beat 1: clap your palm on your thigh.

setup.art: A hand tapping the little finger, then the ring finger, then the middle finger against the thumb, numbered 2, 3 and 4.
setup.caption: 2. Beats 2, 3 and 4: tap your little, ring and middle fingers.

setup.art: A hand clapping palm down, then turned over palm up, twice, numbered 5, 6, 7 and 8.
setup.caption: 3. Beats 5 to 8: clap, turn the hand over, clap, turn it over.

flow.do: Sit down. Keep the tala slowly together, counting out loud from 1 to 8. Beat 1 is a clap on the thigh. Beats 2, 3 and 4 are finger taps. Beats 5 and 7 are claps. Beats 6 and 8 are the hand turned palm up.
flow.say: Clap, little finger, ring finger, middle finger. Clap, turn. Clap, turn. That is 8 beats. Now again, without stopping.
flow.kid: Clap on your thigh. Tap little finger, ring finger, middle finger. Clap, turn your hand over. Clap, turn. Count 1 to 8 as you go.
flow.parent: If you know the tala, lead. If not, learn it together slowly. It takes a few rounds. An even speed matters more than a fast one.
flow.context: This is the first step of clapping Adi tala. A tala is a cycle of beats in South Indian music, and Adi tala has 8 beats.

flow.do: 1. Draw a strip of 8 equal boxes. 2. Colour the boxes for the first section, beats 1 to 4. 3. Colour beats 5 and 6 in a second colour, and beats 7 and 8 in a third.
flow.say: The whole cycle is 8 beats. The first section is 4 beats. What fraction of the cycle is that? What about each short section?
flow.kid: Draw 8 equal boxes in a row. Colour boxes 1 to 4. Use a new colour for 5 and 6. Use another for 7 and 8.

ask.q: The first section fills 4 of the 8 boxes. What fraction of the cycle is it?
good: One half, because 8 beats in 2 equal parts gives 4 each.

ask.q: Each short section is 2 beats. What fraction is that?
good: One quarter, because 8 beats in 4 equal parts gives 2 each.

check.q: Adi tala has 8 beats. One beat is what fraction of the cycle?
check.why: The cycle is the whole. It has 8 equal beats. One of 8 equal parts is one eighth. Picking 'eight' usually means giving the number of parts and not the fraction.

flow.context: This is the second step of clapping Adi tala, a cycle of 8 beats in South Indian music. You draw the 8 beats as boxes and find the fractions in them.

flow.do: Keep the tala for 4 cycles. Your child says 'half' on beat 1, and 'quarter' on beats 5 and 7.
flow.say: Now say 'half' when the long section starts, and 'quarter' when each short section starts. Keep the beat even.
flow.kid: Keep the tala going. Say 'half' on beat 1. Say 'quarter' on beat 5. Say 'quarter' on beat 7.
flow.think: The beats are equal parts of time, not of paper. How do you know two beats are equal when you cannot lay them side by side?
flow.context: This is the last step of clapping Adi tala, a cycle of 8 beats in South Indian music. You call out the half and the quarters while keeping the beat.

activities.title: My Day in 24 Boxes
activities.context: In this activity you draw one whole day as a strip of 24 boxes, one box for each hour. You colour in what you do, and find what fraction of your day goes to sleeping, eating, learning and playing.
activities.problem: The Earth turns round once in a day. People cut that one day into 24 hours. You will use the hours as equal parts and find fractions of your own day.

materials.item: paper, a ruler, a pencil and 4 or 5 colour pencils

schedule.what: Draw a 24-box strip for one day. Colour it by what you do. Name the fractions.

activities.record: Under your strip, write a fraction of the day for at least three things, such as 'Sleep: 8 hours, one third of my day'.

setup.art: A long strip of 24 equal boxes drawn with a ruler, each box 1 cm wide, numbered with the hours.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a strip 24 cm long. Mark 24 boxes, one for each hour.

setup.art: The same strip with 8 boxes coloured dark blue for sleep and other blocks in green, yellow and red.
setup.caption: 2. Colour the hours by what you do in them.

setup.art: A child counting 8 blue boxes and writing 'one third' under them.
setup.caption: 3. Count the boxes of each colour. Name the fraction of the day.

flow.do: Draw a strip 24 cm long and 2 cm tall. Mark a line at every centimetre, to make 24 boxes. Explain that each box is one hour.
flow.say: This strip is one whole day. It has 24 equal boxes. Each box is one hour. What fraction of a day is one hour?
flow.kid: Draw a strip 24 cm long. Mark every centimetre. Now you have 24 boxes. Each box is one hour of the day.

ask.q: What fraction of the day is one hour?
good: One twenty-fourth, because 24 equal parts make the whole day.

flow.context: This is the first step of My Day in 24 Boxes. You draw one whole day as a strip of 24 equal boxes, one for each hour.

flow.do: Talk through an ordinary day. Colour sleep first, then meals, lessons, play and everything else. Round each one to whole hours.
flow.say: How many hours do you sleep? Colour that many boxes. Now meals. Now lessons. Now play.
flow.kid: Colour the hours you sleep. Then colour meals, lessons and play. Use a new colour for each. Count in whole hours.
flow.context: This is the second step of My Day in 24 Boxes, where one day is drawn as a strip of 24 hour boxes. You colour the hours by what you do.

flow.do: Count the boxes of each colour. Use the table from the Strip Test if you did it: 12 boxes is a half, 8 is a third, 6 is a quarter, 4 is a sixth, 3 is an eighth.
flow.say: You coloured 8 boxes for sleep. Can 24 be shared into equal groups of 8? How many groups? So what fraction is sleep?
flow.kid: Count each colour. 12 boxes is one half of the day. 8 boxes is one third. 6 boxes is one quarter. Write your fractions.

ask.q: You sleep for about one third of the day. About how many years of a 9-year life is that?
good: About 3 years, because one third of 9 is 3.

check.q: A day has 24 hours. Sleeping takes 8 hours. What fraction of the day is that?
check.why: 24 hours shared into 3 equal parts gives 8 hours in each part. So 8 hours is one third of the day. Picking 'one eighth' usually means using the 8 hours as the bottom number. The bottom number is the number of equal parts, which is 3.

flow.think: In India, people also cut the day into 60 equal parts called nazhigai. How many minutes is one nazhigai?
flow.context: This is the last step of My Day in 24 Boxes, where one day is drawn as a strip of 24 hour boxes coloured by what you do. You name the fractions of your day.

activities.title: One Quarter, Three Shapes
activities.context: In this activity you fold three squares of paper into quarters in three different ways. Then you cut and fit the pieces on top of each other. You find out whether quarters that look different are the same amount.
activities.problem: Equal parts must be the same amount. You will test whether a quarter shaped like a strip, a quarter shaped like a small square and a quarter shaped like a triangle are equal, when they come from squares of the same size.

materials.item: squares of paper, all the same size, about 12 cm along each side
scissors, a pencil, and a steel tumbler to draw round

schedule.what: Fold three equal squares into quarters three ways. Cut and fit the quarters on each other. Then test a circle cut by side-by-side lines.

activities.record: Stick one quarter of each kind in your notebook and write under them whether they are the same amount, and how you know.

setup.art: Three squares of paper of the same size folded into 4 long strips, 4 small squares and 4 triangles.
setup.caption: 1. Fold three equal squares into quarters, three ways.

setup.art: A triangle quarter cut down the middle into two small triangles, which are being placed onto a small square quarter and cover it exactly.
setup.caption: 2. Cut a triangle quarter in two. Fit the pieces on the square quarter.

setup.art: A paper circle with three straight lines drawn side by side across it, making two thin end pieces and two fat middle pieces.
setup.caption: 3. Draw three lines side by side across a circle. Are these quarters?

flow.do: 1. Fold the first square in half and in half again the same way, to make 4 strips. 2. Fold the second in half one way and then the other way, to make 4 small squares. 3. Fold the third corner to corner both ways, to make 4 triangles. 4. Cut one quarter from each.
flow.say: Each square is in 4 equal parts. Here are three quarters with three shapes. Do you think they are the same amount of paper? Why?
flow.kid: Fold one square into 4 strips. Fold one into 4 small squares. Fold one into 4 triangles. Cut out one quarter of each. Are they the same amount? Guess.

ask.q: Which quarter looks biggest to you? Why?
good: Any answer with a reason. Many people pick the long strip or the triangle.

flow.context: This is the first step of One Quarter, Three Shapes. You fold three squares of paper of the same size into quarters in three different ways.

flow.do: 1. Fold the triangle quarter in half and cut along the fold. Fit the two small triangles onto the small square quarter. 2. Cut the strip quarter in half across its middle. Fit the two short pieces onto the small square quarter.
flow.say: Cut the triangle in two and lay the pieces on the small square. Do they cover it exactly? Now try the strip.
flow.kid: Cut the triangle quarter in two. Lay the pieces on the square quarter. Do they cover it? Now cut the strip in two and try.

ask.q: What does it show when the pieces cover the square exactly?
good: They are the same amount of paper.
The shape is different but the amount is equal.

check.q: Two same-size squares are folded into quarters, one into triangles and one into small squares. Which quarter has more paper?
check.why: Each is one of 4 equal parts of the same square, so each is the same amount. You can cut the triangle in two and the pieces cover the small square exactly. Picking the triangle usually means judging by its longer edge.

flow.context: This is the second step of One Quarter, Three Shapes. You cut quarters of different shapes and fit them on each other to see if they are the same amount.

flow.do: 1. Draw round a tumbler and cut out the circle. 2. Fold the circle in half and in half again the same way, to make 3 fold lines side by side. Cut along them. 3. Lay an end piece on a middle piece.
flow.say: This circle is also in 4 pieces. Are they quarters? Lay an end piece on a middle piece and see.
flow.kid: Cut out a paper circle. Fold it in half, and in half again the same way. Cut on the three folds. Are the 4 pieces equal? Lay one on another.

ask.q: There are 4 pieces. Why are they not quarters?
good: They are not equal. The middle pieces are bigger.
Quarters must be the same amount.

ask.q: How would you cut a circle into real quarters?
good: Fold it in half, then fold the half in half the other way, so the folds cross in the middle.

flow.context: This is the last step of One Quarter, Three Shapes. After testing quarters of a square, you cut a circle into 4 pieces that are not equal, and see why they are not quarters.

projects.title: A Patchwork in Fractions
projects.context: This is a two-day craft project. A patchwork is a cloth made by stitching small pieces together. You plan a paper or cloth patchwork of 24 squares in which each colour is a chosen fraction of the whole.
projects.problem: Quilters and tailors plan how much of each cloth they need before they cut. You will design a patchwork of 24 equal squares. One half must be one colour, one quarter a second, one sixth a third, and one twelfth a fourth.

materials.item: a sheet of thick paper or card, a ruler and a pencil
colour paper in 4 colours, or scraps of old cloth in 4 colours, with scissors and glue
a needle and thread, only if you stitch cloth with a grown-up

projects.safety: Needles are sharp. Stitch only with a grown-up beside you.

schedule.what: Draw the grid of 24 squares. Work out how many squares each colour needs. Cut the squares.
Arrange the squares into a pattern you like. Glue or stitch them. Write the fraction label.

projects.record: Under the finished patchwork, write each colour, its number of squares and its fraction of the whole. Check that the squares add up to 24.

setup.art: A grid of 24 squares, 6 across and 4 down, drawn on card with a ruler, each square 3 cm wide.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a grid of 24 equal squares: 6 across and 4 down.

setup.art: Four small heaps of cut paper squares in four colours: 12 red, 6 blue, 4 yellow and 2 green.
setup.caption: 2. Cut squares in 4 colours: one half, one quarter, one sixth and one twelfth of 24.

setup.art: A finished patchwork of 24 coloured squares in a balanced pattern with a small label of fractions underneath.
setup.caption: 3. Arrange them in a pattern, glue or stitch, and label the fractions.

flow.do: Draw a rectangle 18 cm wide and 12 cm tall on the card. Mark every 3 cm along each side and join the marks. Count the squares together.
flow.say: This grid is our whole patchwork. How many equal squares does it have?
flow.kid: Draw a box 18 cm wide and 12 cm tall. Mark every 3 cm. Join the marks. Count the squares.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Patchwork in Fractions. You draw a grid of 24 equal squares, which will be the whole patchwork.

flow.do: Work out the number of squares for each colour before cutting. Ask your child to find one half, one quarter, one sixth and one twelfth of 24. Use 24 seeds if needed.
flow.say: One colour must be one half of the 24 squares. How many is that? Now one quarter. Now one sixth. Now one twelfth.
flow.kid: Find one half of 24. Find one quarter of 24. Find one sixth of 24. Find one twelfth of 24. Write the four numbers.

ask.q: Add your four numbers. What do you get, and what does that tell you?
good: 12 and 6 and 4 and 2 make 24.
The four fractions use up the whole patchwork exactly.

check.q: A patchwork has 24 squares. One sixth of them are yellow. How many squares are yellow?
check.why: Share 24 into 6 equal groups and each group has 4. So one sixth of 24 is 4. Picking 6 usually means using the bottom number as the answer. Picking 18 means taking 6 away from 24.

flow.context: This is the second step of A Patchwork in Fractions, a patchwork of 24 squares. You work out how many squares each colour needs from its fraction.

flow.do: Cut 3 cm squares from the colour paper or cloth: 12 of the first colour, 6 of the second, 4 of the third and 2 of the fourth.
flow.say: Cut 12 of this colour, 6 of this, 4 of this and 2 of this. Each square is 3 cm along each side.
flow.kid: Cut squares 3 cm wide. Cut 12 of one colour and 6 of the next. Then cut 4 and 2 of the last two colours.
flow.context: This is the third step of A Patchwork in Fractions, a patchwork of 24 squares in four colours. You cut the squares.

flow.do: On the second day, lay the squares on the grid and move them about until the pattern pleases your child. Then glue them down, or stitch cloth squares together with a grown-up.
flow.say: Try a few patterns before you glue. The fractions stay the same whatever pattern you choose. Why is that?
flow.kid: Lay your squares on the grid. Try different patterns. Pick the one you like best. Glue the squares down.

ask.q: If you move the squares around, does the fraction of each colour change?
good: No. There are still 12, 6, 4 and 2 squares out of 24.

flow.context: This is the fourth step of A Patchwork in Fractions, a patchwork of 24 squares in four colours. You arrange the squares into a pattern and fix them.

flow.do: Write a label under the patchwork with each colour, its number of squares and its fraction. Ask one last question about a bigger patchwork.
flow.say: Write the label. Then tell me this. If the patchwork had 48 squares, how many would the half colour need?
flow.kid: Write a label. Put each colour, its squares and its fraction. Then think: what if there were 48 squares?
flow.think: A tailor has only half as much red cloth as you used. What is the biggest patchwork she can make with the same fractions?
flow.context: This is the last step of A Patchwork in Fractions, a patchwork of 24 squares in which each colour is a fraction of the whole. You label the fractions.

challenges.title: Three Dosas, Four People
challenges.context: This is a sharing puzzle that goes a step further than unit fractions. Three dosas must be shared equally among four people. You use paper circles as the dosas and look for more than one way to do it.
challenges.problem: Four people sit down to eat, and there are only 3 dosas, all the same size. Share them so that everyone gets exactly the same amount, with nothing left over. Then say what fraction of a dosa each person gets.
constraints: Every person must get the same amount of dosa.
All 3 dosas must be used up.
You may cut a dosa only into equal parts.
materials: 3 paper circles of the same size (draw round a small plate), scissors and a pencil
4 small plates or 4 sheets of paper, one for each person
general: Cut every dosa into 4 equal quarters. That makes 12 quarters. Give each person 3 quarters, one from each dosa.
Each person gets three quarters of a dosa, written 3/4.
creative: Cut 2 dosas into halves. That makes 4 halves, one for each person. Cut the last dosa into quarters, one for each person. Each person gets one half and one quarter.
This is how scribes in Egypt wrote three quarters about 3,500 years ago: as one half and one quarter together.
challenges.your_turn: Now make up your own sharing puzzle with a different number of dosas and people, such as 2 dosas for 3 people. Solve it with paper circles, and say what each person gets.

setup.art: Three paper circles and four small empty plates on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Three dosas, four plates. Everyone must get the same.

setup.art: Three paper circles each cut like a cross into 4 quarters, with 3 quarters placed on each of four plates.
setup.caption: 2. One way: cut every dosa into quarters. Give 3 quarters to each plate.

setup.art: Four plates each holding one half circle and one quarter circle.
setup.caption: 3. Another way: a half and a quarter on each plate.

flow.do: Cut out 3 paper circles and lay out 4 plates. Read the problem. Ask for a first idea before any cutting.
flow.say: Three dosas, four people, and everyone must get the same. Will each person get more than one dosa or less than one? How do you know?
flow.kid: You have 3 dosas and 4 people. Everyone must get the same. Will each person get a whole dosa? Say what you think.

ask.q: Will each person get more than half a dosa or less than half?
good: More than half. Two dosas already give everyone a half, and there is one more dosa to share.

flow.context: This is the first step of the puzzle Three Dosas, Four People. Three paper dosas must be shared equally among four plates.

flow.do: Let your child try. Give no method. If they are stuck after a few minutes, ask: 'What if you had only 1 dosa for 4 people?'
flow.say: Try it your way with the paper dosas. You can fold and cut. Check that every plate has the same amount.
flow.kid: Fold and cut the paper dosas. Put the pieces on the 4 plates. Check that every plate has the same amount.
flow.parent: Both ways in this challenge are good. Many children find the quarters way first. Some give halves first and then share out the last dosa. Praise any way that gives equal plates.
flow.context: This is the second step of the puzzle Three Dosas, Four People. You try your own way of sharing three paper dosas equally among four plates.

flow.do: Look at one plate together. Count the pieces and name them. Then show the other way, using 3 fresh circles, and compare a plate from each way.
flow.say: What is on one plate? Name each piece. Here is another way to share. Is a plate from this way the same amount as a plate from yours?
flow.kid: Look at one plate. Name each piece. Now try the other way with new circles. Lay the pieces from one plate on the other. Are they the same amount?

ask.q: One plate has 3 quarters. Another has 1 half and 1 quarter. Are they the same amount?
good: Yes. A half covers two quarters exactly, so both plates have three quarters.

check.q: Three dosas are shared equally among 4 people. How much does each person get?
check.why: Cut each dosa into 4 quarters and you have 12 quarters. Shared among 4 people, that is 3 quarters each. Picking 'one quarter' usually means sharing only one of the dosas.

flow.context: This is the third step of the puzzle Three Dosas, Four People. You compare two ways of sharing three paper dosas equally among four plates.

flow.do: Ask your child to make up a new sharing puzzle and solve it with paper circles.
flow.say: Now you set a puzzle for me. Choose the number of dosas and the number of people.
flow.kid: Make up your own puzzle. Choose how many dosas and how many people. Solve it with paper circles.
flow.think: Is there a number of dosas and people where nobody needs to cut anything?
flow.context: This is the last step of the puzzle Three Dosas, Four People, in which paper dosas are shared equally. You invent your own sharing puzzle.

challenges.title: I Cut, You Choose
challenges.context: This is a fairness puzzle for two people. One thing with an odd shape, such as a banana or a lump of dough, must be shared in two so that both people are happy. You test a very old rule: one person cuts and the other chooses.
challenges.problem: It is easy to cut a paper strip into halves, because you can fold it. A banana, a mango or a lump of dough has no fold line. Find a way for two people to share one so that neither can say the other got more.
constraints: There is no ruler and no weighing scale.
Both people must agree it was fair before anyone eats.
materials: one banana, or a lump of chapati dough or play dough about the size of a lemon
a blunt butter knife and a plate
general: One person cuts and the other chooses first. The cutter then tries hard to make the two parts equal, because the cutter gets the part that is left.
Check afterwards by laying the parts side by side, or by holding one in each hand.
creative: Roll the dough into an even snake first. Then fold a thread to find the middle of its length.
With 3 people it is harder. One way: the first person cuts off what they think is one third. Anyone who thinks it is too big may trim it. The last person to touch a piece keeps it.
challenges.your_turn: Find your own rule for 3 people to share one lump of dough so that nobody complains. Try it with real people. Did it work?
challenges.safety: Use a blunt butter knife, not a sharp one.

setup.art: Two children sitting on either side of a plate with one banana and a butter knife.
setup.caption: 1. One banana, two people, one cut.

setup.art: One child cutting the banana very carefully near the middle while the other watches closely.
setup.caption: 2. One person cuts. The other person chooses first.

setup.art: Two pieces of banana laid side by side to compare their lengths.
setup.caption: 3. Lay the parts side by side. Were they equal?

flow.do: Put the banana or dough on a plate between two people. Ask how to share it so both are happy. Listen to every idea.
flow.say: We have one banana and two people. There is no ruler. How can we share it so neither of us can complain?
flow.kid: One banana. Two people. No ruler. How can you share it so nobody complains? Say your ideas.
flow.context: This is the first step of the puzzle I Cut, You Choose. Two people must share one banana or lump of dough fairly, with no ruler.

flow.do: Try the rule. Your child cuts, and you choose first. Then swap with a second banana or a fresh lump of dough, so you cut and your child chooses.
flow.say: You cut, and I choose first. Think about where to cut. Then we swap.
flow.kid: You cut. The other person chooses first. Cut carefully. Then swap over and try again.

ask.q: When you were the cutter, why did you try to make the parts equal?
good: Because the other person would take the bigger part and I would get the smaller one.

flow.context: This is the second step of the puzzle I Cut, You Choose. One person cuts a banana or lump of dough in two, and the other person chooses a part first.

flow.do: Lay the two parts side by side. Ask whether they are equal, and equal in what way: length, thickness or weight.
flow.say: Are these two halves? How can we tell? Is the longer one always the bigger one?
flow.kid: Lay the two parts side by side. Are they equal? Is the longer part always the bigger part?

ask.q: A banana is thin at the ends and fat in the middle. Is half the length always half the banana?
good: Not always. A short fat part can be as much as a long thin part.

check.q: In 'I cut, you choose', why does the cutter try to cut two equal parts?
options: The cutter gets the part that is left
The cutter always gets the bigger part
The rule says to use a ruler
check.why: The chooser picks first and will take the bigger part if there is one. So the cutter does best by making the parts as equal as possible. No ruler is needed.

flow.context: This is the third step of the puzzle I Cut, You Choose, in which one person cuts a banana in two and the other chooses first. You check whether the parts were equal.

flow.do: Ask how the rule could work for 3 people. Try an idea with dough if there is a third person at home.
flow.say: This rule works for two. What could three people do? Try your idea with the dough.
flow.kid: The rule works for 2 people. What could 3 people do? Think of a rule. Try it with dough.
flow.think: Two people can both feel they got the bigger half. How can that be?
flow.context: This is the last step of the puzzle I Cut, You Choose, about sharing one thing fairly between two people. You look for a rule that works for three people.
