quiz.p: Which of these shows one third?
opts: A roti cut into 3 equal pieces, 1 taken
A roti cut into 3 unequal pieces, 1 taken
quiz.why: One third is one of 3 equal parts of a whole. Unequal pieces are not thirds. Three whole rotis are three wholes, not a fraction.

quiz.p: If a whole is split into parts that are not equal, the parts cannot be named as halves, thirds or quarters.
quiz.why: True. The names of fractions only work for equal parts. Two unequal pieces are 'a big piece and a small piece', not two halves.
One part goes on top. The 6 equal parts of the whole go underneath. Picking 6/1 puts the numbers the wrong way up.

quiz.p: In the fraction 1/8, what does the 8 tell you?
opts: How many equal parts make the whole
quiz.why: The bottom number counts the equal parts in the whole. The top number counts the parts you have. The bottom number is not a size. A bigger bottom number means smaller parts.

quiz.p: Three idlis of the same size are cut up. Which piece is biggest?
quiz.why: The idlis are the same size. The one cut into only 2 equal parts has the biggest parts. Picking 1/10 usually means reading the 10 as a size.

quiz.p: Cutting the same cake into more equal pieces makes each piece smaller.
quiz.why: True. The cake does not grow, so more pieces must share the same amount, and each gets less.

quiz.p: One quarter of 16 tamarind seeds is ____ seeds.
quiz.why: Share 16 into 4 equal groups. Each group has 4. So one quarter of 16 is 4.

quiz.p: What is one fifth of 15 rupees?
quiz.why: Share 15 into 5 equal groups. Each group has 3. Picking 5 usually means using the bottom number as the answer. Picking 10 means taking 5 away. Picking 75 means multiplying.

quiz.p: What do you do to find one third of 21 shells?
opts: Share 21 into 3 equal groups, count one
Share 21 into 7 equal groups, count one
quiz.why: The bottom number is 3, so make 3 equal groups. Each has 7 shells. One group is one third. Taking 3 away is subtraction, which answers a different question.

quiz.p: Which is more: one half of 8 laddus or one quarter of 40 laddus?
quiz.why: One half of 8 is 4 laddus. One quarter of 40 is 10 laddus. The wholes are different, so the bigger fraction does not give the bigger amount.

quiz.p: Someone offers you 'one quarter'. What must you ask before you know how much you will get?
opts: Is a quarter more than a half?
How do you write a quarter?
quiz.why: A quarter is one of 4 equal parts of some whole. Until you know the whole, you do not know the amount. A quarter of a kilogram and a quarter of a spoonful are very different.

quiz.p: One paper square is folded into 4 triangles. Another like it is folded into 4 small squares. Which part has more paper?
quiz.why: Each is one quarter of the same size of square, so they are the same amount of paper. Equal parts need the same amount, not the same shape.

quiz.p: A bowl is narrow at the bottom and wide at the top. Water half-way up it is half of a full bowl.
quiz.why: False. The narrow bottom half holds less than the wide top half. Height shows the amount only when the sides are straight.

quiz.p: Which of these did people choose, so that it could have been different?
opts: Four quarters of a thing make the whole thing
1/8 of a strip is shorter than 1/3 of it
quiz.why: The way of writing is a choice. Egyptian scribes and Indian mathematicians wrote fractions differently. The other two follow from what a fraction means, whoever does the sum and however they write it.

quiz.p: Why does a day have 24 hours?
opts: People long ago chose to cut the day into 24 parts
The Earth turns 24 times in a day
quiz.why: The Earth turns once in a day. Cutting that one turn into 24 equal parts was a choice. In India people also cut the day into 60 parts called nazhigai.

applications: Markets: 'kaal kilo' is a quarter of a kilogram and 'arai kilo' is half. Shopkeepers weigh these fractions all day.
Cooking: half a cup of rice, a quarter of a spoon of turmeric, three quarters of a glass of water.
Telling the time: half past, a quarter past and a quarter to are fractions of an hour.
Music and dance: a tala is a cycle of beats, and its sections are fractions of the cycle.
Money: a 50 paise coin was half a rupee. 'Half price' means one half of the price.
Tailoring and patchwork: a tailor folds cloth in half and in quarters to find the middle and to cut equal panels.
Sharing food: one dosa for 2, a packet of 12 biscuits for 4, a watermelon for 8.
Medicine: a doctor may tell a grown-up to give half a tablet. The tablet has a line so it breaks into equal parts.
Sport: a football match has two halves. Many basketball and kabaddi matches are split into halves or quarters of equal time.
Astronomy: the first quarter and last quarter Moon are named for fractions of the Moon's trip round the Earth.
Buses and trains: a child's 'half ticket' costs about half of the full fare.
Farming and land: old Tamil land records used small fractions with their own names, such as mundiri, 1 part in 320.

open_questions.q: Can space itself be cut in half for ever?
open_questions.why_open: Numbers can always be halved. Real stuff cannot, because it is made of particles. For space itself, some physicists think there may be a smallest length. No experiment has shown whether there is.

open_questions.q: When a chimpanzee or a chick picks out a half or a proportion, what is it like for them?
open_questions.why_open: Experiments show what these animals choose. They do not show what the animals experience, or whether a half means to them what it means to us.

open_questions.q: Were fractions invented by people, or discovered?
open_questions.why_open: Mathematicians and philosophers have argued about this for more than 2,000 years. Both sides have good reasons, and no test has been found that would settle it.

open_questions.q: Why did Egyptian scribes write nearly every fraction as a sum of unit fractions?
open_questions.why_open: The scribes left tables of answers but no explanation of why they worked this way. Historians have several ideas and no record that decides between them.

The clock says a quarter past. A quarter of what?
This packet has 12 biscuits. What is one third of the packet?
Is half of your glass more than half of my glass?
How many quarter-kilo bags make one kilo?

You have eaten half your idlis. What fraction is left?

If you fold this paper in half 3 times, how many parts will there be? Guess, then try.

jokes.j: Why did the half say no to another cut?

maths.problem: Tomatoes cost 40 rupees for one kilogram. How much does a quarter of a kilogram cost?
maths.explain: A quarter is one of 4 equal parts. Share the 40 rupees into 4 equal parts. 40 divided by 4 is 10. So a quarter of a kilogram costs 10 rupees.
maths.context: In markets in Tamil Nadu, people ask for 'kaal kilo', which means a quarter of a kilogram. This problem uses what you learned about finding one quarter of an amount.
maths.why_maths: A price is usually given for a whole kilogram. To pay for a part, you need the same fraction of the price.

maths.problem: You shared 24 groundnuts into 8 equal groups and found 3 in each group. Write this as a fraction sentence and as a division sentence.
maths.answer: One eighth of 24 is 3. 24 divided by 8 is 3.
maths.explain: Sharing 24 into 8 equal groups is division: 24 divided by 8 is 3. One of those groups is one eighth of the 24. So the two sentences say the same thing in two ways.
maths.context: In the Strip Test you shared 24 groundnuts into 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 equal groups and counted one group each time.
maths.why_maths: Finding a unit fraction of a group and dividing are the same action. If you know your division facts, you already know these fractions.

maths.problem: An hour has 60 minutes. How many minutes are in a quarter of an hour, and in three quarters of an hour?
maths.explain: Share 60 minutes into 4 equal parts. 60 divided by 4 is 15. So a quarter of an hour is 15 minutes. Three quarters is 3 lots of 15 minutes, which is 45 minutes.
maths.context: People say 'a quarter past four' and 'a quarter to five'. The whole is one hour, and the clock face is cut into 4 equal parts.
maths.why_maths: Clock words such as 'half past' and 'quarter to' are fractions of an hour. Knowing the fraction tells you the minutes.

maths.problem: A glass holds 200 millilitres. Your neer mor is one quarter curd and the rest water. How many millilitres of curd and of water do you need?
maths.answer: 50 millilitres of curd and 150 millilitres of water.
maths.explain: Share 200 into 4 equal parts. 200 divided by 4 is 50. One part is curd, so the curd is 50 millilitres. The other 3 parts are water. 3 lots of 50 is 150 millilitres.
maths.context: Neer mor is a thin salted buttermilk. In the cooking activity you made it with one quarter of a glass of curd and three quarters of a glass of water.
maths.why_maths: A recipe in fractions works for any size of glass. To use a measuring jug, you turn the fraction into millilitres.

maths.problem: You start with 32 groundnuts. Each day you eat half of what is left. How many are left after each day? On which day is only 1 left?
maths.answer: 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. One groundnut is left after day 5.
maths.explain: Half of 32 is 16. Half of 16 is 8. Half of 8 is 4. Half of 4 is 2. Half of 2 is 1. That is 5 halvings. Each number is half of the one before it.
maths.context: When you fold a paper strip in half again and again, each part is half the size of the one before. This problem does the same with a heap of 32 groundnuts.
maths.why_maths: Halving again and again makes a number pattern. Seeing the pattern lets you say what comes next without counting.

maths.problem: A ribbon is 1 metre long, which is 100 centimetres. It is cut into 5 equal pieces. How long is each piece, and what fraction of the ribbon is it?
maths.answer: Each piece is 20 centimetres long. It is one fifth of the ribbon.
maths.explain: Share 100 centimetres into 5 equal parts. 100 divided by 5 is 20. One of 5 equal parts is one fifth. You can check: 5 pieces of 20 centimetres make 100 centimetres.
maths.context: In the Strip Test you cut 24 cm paper strips into equal parts and measured one part. This problem does the same with a longer ribbon.
maths.why_maths: Cutting a length into equal parts is how tailors and carpenters work. The fraction tells you how many pieces, and the division tells you how long each is.

roots.context: We have been cutting strips and sharing groundnuts into equal parts. Now we ask what a fraction tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Take 24 groundnuts and 12 groundnuts. One quarter of 24 is 6. One quarter of 12 is 3. It is the same 'one quarter', but the amounts differ. A fraction does not say how much. It says how much of what.
deep_truth.habit: We think one quarter is a fixed amount, like 4 groundnuts. It is not. It always means one quarter of something, and a person chooses that something.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Strip Test, one quarter of 24 was 6 and one quarter of 12 was 3. In the card game Bigger Share, one eighth of 40 beat one half of 4.

three.who_am_i: You are one whole person. You are also one part of your family, and one of more than eight billion people. Each is true for a different whole.
three.what_is_life: One living cell divides into two, and each half grows into a whole cell. In living beings, a part can become a whole.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth turns once, and nothing marks that turn into parts. People cut it into 24 hours, or into 60 nazhigai.

roots.thread: A fraction starts with one whole thing. Cut it into parts and put the parts back together: you get the same whole. Any part can be picked up, called 'one', and cut again. Which thing we call 'one' is our choice. What follows from that choice is the same for everyone.

teachings.source: Isha Upanishad, opening verse (also Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.1.1)
teachings.teaching: That is whole, this is whole. From the whole the whole comes out. Take the whole from the whole, and the whole remains.
teachings.link: The verse is about the whole of everything, not about dosas. The small parallel in this lesson is that a part taken from a whole can itself be treated as a whole. In the story, the last quarter of the jaggery became the new whole and was cut into fifths.

teachings.teaching: Take a stick one foot long. Each day, take away half of what is left. Even after ten thousand generations it will not be used up.
teachings.link: This is the halving you did by folding: one half, one quarter, one eighth. With numbers there is always another half to take. With a real stick, the pieces at last become too small to cut.

science.text: Numbers can be halved without end, but real stuff cannot. Cut a grain of sugar small enough and you reach single molecules. Cut a molecule and the pieces are no longer sugar.
Some physicists think space itself may have a smallest possible length, so that it could not be halved for ever. No experiment has shown this.

other_view.who: Platonists: many mathematicians and philosophers, named after the Greek thinker Plato
other_view.view: They say that numbers and fractions exist by themselves, whether or not anyone thinks about them. People choose the names and the signs, but one quarter of a thing would be one quarter of it even if no person had ever lived. On this view, people discover mathematics. They do not make it.

how_we_found_out.story: About 3,500 years ago in Egypt, a scribe called Ahmes copied out a book of sums. Today it is called the Rhind papyrus. In it, nearly every fraction is a unit fraction, with 1 on top. The scribes had a special sign for two thirds, but they wrote three quarters as one half and one quarter. In Greece, about 2,300 years ago, Euclid wrote that a number is a collection of ones. On that view, the one cannot be broken, so a fraction is not a number at all. Mathematicians in India worked differently. By the year 628, Brahmagupta wrote fractions as one number above another, with any number on top, and added and multiplied them like other numbers. About 850, Mahavira, a Jain mathematician who probably worked at the Rashtrakuta court in the Deccan, gave rules for turning a fraction into a sum of unit fractions. Arab mathematicians later added the line between the two numbers. In 1585, Simon Stevin, from Flanders, argued that every quantity is a number, fractions included. That is how fractions are treated today.
how_we_found_out.who: The scribe Ahmes, Brahmagupta, Mahavira, Arab mathematicians such as al-Hassar, and Simon Stevin
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Greek mathematicians held that the one cannot be divided, so a fraction is not a number. People gave this up because fractions can be added, compared and put in order just like whole numbers. It was a change in what people agreed to call a number.
